docs.text: Free Will “Free will” can name several questions. A philosopher may ask what makes an action up to the agent . A theologian may ask how a creature acts under divine providence, or whether a fallen person can respond to God without prior grace. These questions overlap, but none should be silently substituted for another. The central questions Could I have done otherwise? Did the action genuinely come from me? Was I acting voluntarily rather than under relevant coercion? Can causal determinism coexist with freedom or responsibility? If an action is undetermined, what gives the agent control over it? Does infallible divine foreknowledge make the future necessary? Can God ordain an event while the human action remains voluntary? Can fallen humans turn toward God without grace? What must grace do: heal, enable, renew, or infallibly bring about response? Can saving grace be resisted? How are election and predestination understood? Can a true believer finally apostatize? Crucial distinction Philosophical freedom and spiritual ability are different questions. A theologian can affirm meaningful ordinary agency while denying that a fallen sinner can initiate saving faith without prior divine grace. Compatibilism/libertarianism and monergism/synergism are different axes. The first concerns freedom and determination; the second concerns divine and human agency in conversion or salvation. docs.text: Common Confusions About Free Will These corrections identify distinctions, not winners. If God knows it, God caused it Knowledge and causation are different relations. The philosophical problem is whether infallibility plus the fixity of the past makes alternatives impossible, not whether a belief mechanically produces an act. See Foreknowledge and Free Will . If an act is undetermined, it must be random Indeterminism does not entail purposelessness, but neither does it by itself supply control. Agent-causal, event-causal, and non-causal libertarians offer different accounts of ownership. See Libertarian Free Will . Compatibilists do not believe in free will Compatibilists affirm free will while denying that determinism excludes it. Their critics dispute whether voluntariness, ownership, or reasons-responsiveness is enough. See the SEP entry . Calvinists think people are robots Reformed confessions affirm voluntary creaturely agency and describe effectual calling as renewing the will so that a person comes willingly. The dispute is whether this account provides the right control, not whether persons literally lack wills. See Westminster IX–X . Arminians think humans save themselves Arminius says free will cannot begin or perfect true spiritual good without grace; grace precedes, accompanies, and sustains response. See his “Grace and Free Will” . Synergism means salvation is half God and half human Synergy means real cooperation made possible and sustained by indispensable grace. It is not a percentage split or an assertion of equal independent causes. See Grace and Salvation . Lutherans are Calvinists with sacraments Both traditions teach monergistic conversion, but differ on universal grace, means of grace, election, resistance, baptism, and apostasy. Compare Lutheran and Reformed . Catholicism has one theory of free will Catholic doctrine sets boundaries while permitting Thomist/Bañezian, Molinist, and other accounts of efficacy and creaturely causation. See Roman Catholic . The Church Fathers were all Arminian Arminianism belongs to a post-Reformation controversy. Many Fathers are anti-fatalist or synergistic, but they address different questions in different vocabularies. See Church Fathers . Augustine was simply Calvin before Calvin Calvin receives Augustine within a different scriptural, medieval, ecclesial, and Reformation setting. Augustine's development and sacramental/catholic context cannot be erased. See Augustine's legacy . Predestination and fatalism are identical Fatalism says the outcome occurs regardless of deliberation and means. Predestinarian traditions ordinarily treat preaching, warning, faith, and action as means within providence. See Predestination . Foreknowledge and predestination are identical Foreknowledge concerns divine knowledge; predestination concerns divine purpose. Arminian, Molinist, Lutheran, Reformed, Catholic, and Orthodox accounts relate them differently. See Foreknowledge and Predestination . Determinism is fatalism Determinism says the past and laws fix the future. Fatalism says an outcome obtains regardless of what one does. A compatibilist treats deliberation and action as causally relevant parts of how the determined result occurs.

docs.text: Dimensions of Free Will Free will is better treated as a multidimensional space than as a single yes-or-no property. The dimensions below include philosophical questions about agency and theological questions about grace. They should be compared, not collapsed. Dimension Core question Alternative possibilities Could I genuinely have chosen otherwise? Sourcehood Does the action originate appropriately from me? Voluntariness Am I acting according to my will rather than under relevant coercion? Reasons-responsiveness Can my decision-making respond appropriately to reasons? Moral responsibility Can I appropriately be praised or blamed? Causal determination Can a causally determined action still be free? Divine determination Can God ordain an event while human action remains voluntary? Divine foreknowledge Does infallible foreknowledge make the future necessary? Spiritual ability Can fallen humans turn toward God unaided? Grace priority Must grace act before saving faith? Grace efficacy What does grace actually accomplish in the will? Resistibility Can grace be resisted? Regeneration/faith order Does regeneration logically precede faith, follow it, or resist simple sequencing? Monergism/synergism Who acts in conversion, and in what sense? Election Is election conditional, unconditional, corporate, or understood otherwise? Reprobation What is the status of the non-elect, if the system uses this category? Perseverance Can a true believer finally apostatize? Interpretive warning Two theologians can both affirm “free will” while disagreeing on nearly every other dimension in this table. Dimensions of agency Alternative possibilities This is leeway : at the relevant moment, was more than one course of action genuinely open? Many libertarian accounts require robust alternatives. Some compatibilists analyze “could have done otherwise” conditionally; other theories deny that alternatives are necessary for responsibility. Frankfurt-style cases are designed to separate responsibility from alternatives. Sourcehood Sourcehood asks whether the action issues from the agent in the right way. A person might lack alternatives yet still act from their own values; conversely, an indeterministic event might offer alternatives without being sufficiently controlled by the agent. This is why sourcehood and alternatives are distinct. Voluntariness An action is voluntary when it proceeds through the person's will rather than through the relevant kind of external force. Voluntariness alone may be too weak: manipulation can produce willing action while raising doubts about ownership of the motives. Reasons-responsiveness A reasons-responsive mechanism can recognize relevant reasons and modify action across an appropriate range of possible situations. This idea is central to influential compatibilist accounts, but theories disagree about how much responsiveness and ownership are required. Moral responsibility Responsibility may mean basic-desert praise or blame, accountability within relationships, or forward-looking practices such as protection and moral formation. Conclusions about free will can change with the kind of responsibility at issue. See Moral Responsibility . Dimensions of determination and knowledge Causal determination Causal determinism says that the total past together with the laws of nature fixes one future. Compatibilists say this can coexist with the relevant freedom; incompatibilists deny it. Determinism is not fatalism : on a deterministic account, deliberation may itself help cause the outcome. Divine determination Theological systems differ over how divine willing, primary causation, concurrence, permission, and creaturely secondary causes relate. Divine determination is neither automatically identical to physical determinism nor automatically coercive. Divine foreknowledge Infallible knowledge appears to fix what will happen, but knowledge is not itself causation. The main problem concerns necessity, the fixity of the past, and the dependence between a true future act and divine knowledge. See Foreknowledge and Predestination . Dimensions of sin and grace Spiritual ability This asks a narrower question than ordinary agency: can a fallen person, without grace, initiate a saving response to God? Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, Arminian, Wesleyan, Anglican, Baptist, and Pentecostal sources considered in this wiki all give grace an indispensable role, while disagreeing sharply about what follows. Grace priority “Prevenient” literally means preceding. Traditions may affirm that grace precedes faith while differing about whether it is sacramentally mediated, universally enabling, effectual for the elect, or described through another framework. Grace efficacy Grace may be described as healing and elevating nature, illuminating and enabling a response, renewing desire, effectually calling, regenerating, or divinizing. The same word grace therefore cannot be compared without examining its claimed effect. Resistibility One must specify which grace. Reformed theology distinguishes a general gospel call from effectual calling. Lutheran sources affirm monergistic conversion yet also speak of resistance and apostasy. Catholic theology distinguishes sufficient and efficacious grace, with internal schools explaining their relation differently. Regeneration and faith order Some Reformed accounts place regeneration logically before faith; many Arminian and Wesleyan accounts describe prevenient grace before faith and regeneration in connection with faith. Baptismal and sacramental frameworks complicate a simple temporal sequence. “Logical priority” should not be mistaken for a measurable interval. Monergism and synergism Monergism assigns the regenerating or converting act to God alone in the relevant sense. Synergism affirms indispensable prior grace and real human cooperation. This axis does not settle whether ordinary action is libertarian or compatibilist. Election and reprobation Election may be understood as unconditional, conditional on foreknown faith, corporate and Christocentric, sacramental/ecclesial, or in combinations. Reprobation may mean a positive decree, a passing over, permission, or simply the condemned state of persistent unbelief; these are not equivalent. Perseverance Theories range from guaranteed preservation of all the regenerate, through confidence conditioned on continuing faith, to sacramental accounts in which grace can be forfeited and restored. See Perseverance and Apostasy . Sources and next steps The distinction between alternatives and sourcehood follows the SEP overview . Compare the philosophical positions , then use the same dimensions in the thinker and tradition matrices .

docs.text: Foreknowledge and Predestination Foreknowledge concerns what God knows; predestination concerns divine purpose or appointment. Neither is identical to causation, fatalism, or generic causal determinism. Foreknowledge The classic problem asks: If God infallibly knows that I will choose A tomorrow, can I choose B? Foreknowledge does not cause the act merely by being knowledge. The pressure instead comes from infallibility and the apparent necessity of the past : no one can now make a past divine belief false. Philosophers debate whether past beliefs about future choices have the same accidental necessity as wholly past events. Major approaches Approach Central proposal Characteristic question Atemporal/Boethian God knows all times in an eternal present, not by earlier beliefs Does removing temporal priority remove the necessity problem? Ockhamist Some past facts are “soft,” partly about or dependent on the future Which past facts are accidentally necessary? Simple foreknowledge God knows the actual future without middle knowledge How does foreknowledge contribute to providential planning? Molinism God knows what free creatures would do in any feasible circumstance before choosing a world What grounds counterfactuals of creaturely freedom? Open theism The future includes genuine possibilities not yet settled as definite acts How should omniscience and prophecy be understood? Middle knowledge is logically between God's natural knowledge of necessities and free knowledge of the world God decrees to create. Its characteristic objects are counterfactuals of creaturely freedom : claims about what a creature would freely do in specified circumstances. Molina uses these truths to combine providential selection of a world with libertarian creaturely action. Critics debate their grounding and whether God can use them without compromising freedom. Open theists affirm omniscience but argue that at least some future free actions are possibilities rather than already definite truths. The position is internally diverse and should not be reduced to “God guesses.” Classical theists dispute its account of knowledge and providence. The current SEP foreknowledge entry analyzes necessity, eternity, Ockhamism, dependence, and PAP; its categories are philosophical tools, not denominational labels. Predestination Predestination refers to God's eternal purpose regarding salvation and, in some accounts, the ordering of all events. Its object, basis, and mode differ across traditions. Later Augustine: election, the beginning of faith, and final perseverance are gifts not grounded in foreseen merit. Thomism: predestination belongs to providence; God moves creatures according to their created modes and establishes real secondary causation. Reformed: confessional accounts teach unconditional election and effectual calling; many later Reformed theologians use compatibilist analyses. Lutheran: election is to salvation in Christ; the Formula of Concord rejects speculation about a symmetrical decree of damnation and locates condemnation in sin and unbelief. Arminian: election is commonly conditional on divinely foreknown faith, while the ability to believe remains dependent on grace. Wesleyan: election is Christ-centered and conditional, combined with universal prevenient grace and the possibility of apostasy. Eastern Orthodox: predestination is normally framed through foreknowledge, providence, and the divine desire for salvation without an unconditional decree that overrides response. Roman Catholic: predestination is affirmed; God predestines no one to evil or damnation. Thomist/Bañezian and Molinist schools disagree about its metaphysical explanation within common doctrinal boundaries. See the tradition comparison for authoritative sources and qualifications. Double predestination “Double predestination” is ambiguous: A symmetrical account would make election and reprobation parallel positive acts in the same way. Asymmetrical Reformed formulations distinguish God's effective election from passing over or judicial condemnation for sin. Even where both are within a decree, their causal and moral modes are not treated as equal. Lutheran confessions teach election to salvation but reject making God the cause of sin or damnation. Catholic teaching affirms providence and predestination while explicitly denying that God predestines anyone to hell; willful turning from God and persistence are required. The label should therefore never replace analysis of election, passing over, permission, hardening, and judgment. Key distinctions Foreknowledge is not causation. Knowing and causing are conceptually different, even if a theory relates them through providence. Predestination is not foreknowledge. A divine purpose is not merely awareness of an outcome. Predestination is not identical to determinism. Traditions combine it with different accounts of creaturely causation and freedom. Determinism is not fatalism. Deliberation can be causally relevant even if the outcome is determined. Confessional Reformed evaluation The survey above distinguishes the models without ranking them. The dedicated Reformed evaluation argues that unconditional election and comprehensive providence best explain the cumulative pattern of divine purpose, effectual calling, faith, and perseverance, while treating universal-saving-will and apostasy texts as serious counterevidence. docs.text: Glossary Definitions are concise and comparative. Follow the links for disputes and tradition-specific uses. Agency and responsibility Free will A significant kind of control over action, analyzed through alternatives, sourcehood, voluntariness, reasons, or their relation to responsibility. It is not one universally agreed faculty. Liberty Freedom from a relevant constraint or freedom for self-directed action. Theological writers may call obedience to the good a higher liberty than indifferent choice. Determinism The thesis that the complete past plus laws of nature fixes a single future. It is not fatalism . Indeterminism Denial that the relevant history and laws determine a unique outcome. Indeterminism alone does not establish agency or control. Fatalism The thesis that an outcome will occur regardless of deliberation or action. In deterministic theories, by contrast, deliberation can be part of the causal route. Libertarianism The conjunction of free will and incompatibilism: relevant freedom exists and cannot coexist with determinism. See Philosophical Views . Compatibilism The thesis that relevant freedom can coexist with determinism, often analyzed through voluntariness, ownership, or reasons-responsiveness. Incompatibilism The thesis that determinism is incompatible with the relevant freedom. Libertarians and hard determinists are both incompatibilists. Hard determinism Acceptance of determinism combined with denial of free will of the required kind. Hard incompatibilism The view that neither deterministic nor indeterministic causation supplies the control needed for strong freedom or basic-desert responsibility. Free-will skepticism A family of views denying, doubting, or suspending judgment about the kind of free will often thought to ground basic desert. Semi-compatibilism The view that moral responsibility may be compatible with determinism even if the freedom to do otherwise is not. Sourcehood The condition that an action originate from the agent in the right way, rather than merely occurring in or through them. Alternative possibilities Genuinely accessible different actions or choices—often expressed as the ability to do otherwise. Principle of Alternative Possibilities The proposed principle that a person is morally responsible only if they could have done otherwise. Frankfurt-style cases challenge it. Reasons-responsiveness The capacity of an agent or action-producing mechanism to recognize and react appropriately to reasons across a suitable range. Agent causation A libertarian proposal on which a substance or agent, not merely prior events, causes a free action in a distinctive way. Moral responsibility An agent's eligibility for praise, blame, accountability, or other moral responses. Basic desert, attributability, and practical responsibility should be distinguished. Coercion Threat or pressure that makes refusal unreasonably costly and can diminish responsibility without always removing intentional choice. Providence and knowledge Providence Divine preservation and governance of creation, formulated differently through primary/secondary causation, concurrence, permission, middle knowledge, or other models. Foreknowledge Knowledge of future events. Infallibility creates a modal problem about necessity, but knowledge is not identical to causation. Predestination Divine purpose or appointment concerning salvation and, in some systems, the ordering of events. It is not identical to foreknowledge or determinism. Election Divine choosing of a people or persons in Christ, interpreted as unconditional, conditional, corporate, sacramental/ecclesial, or in combinations. Reprobation The non-election or condemnation of the lost, variously described as passing over, permission, judicial hardening, or a decree. The descriptions are not equivalent. Middle knowledge In Molinism, God's logically pre-decretal knowledge of true counterfactuals of creaturely freedom, “middle” between natural and free knowledge. Counterfactuals of creaturely freedom Claims about what a possible free creature would do in specified circumstances, central to Molinist providence. Sin, grace, and salvation Original sin Western term for humanity's fallen condition and solidarity with Adam, including deprivation/corruption and, in several accounts, inherited guilt. Traditions define its elements differently. Ancestral sin Common Eastern term emphasizing inherited mortality, corruption, and disordered conditions from Adam; its contrast with “original sin” should not be exaggerated into a universal East/West formula. Total inability The claim that fallen people cannot turn to God savingly by natural power. It does not mean inability to reason or perform any civic good. Moral inability Inability rooted in a contrary disposition or inclination rather than missing natural faculties or opportunity; especially important in Edwards. Grace God's free favor, help, action, gift, or communicated life. The term's precise effect and metaphysics differ across traditions. Prevenient grace Grace that goes before response. In Wesleyan theology it universally enables a saving response without making it inevitable. Sufficient grace In Catholic debates, grace genuinely sufficient for a salutary act; schools dispute how it relates to efficacious grace and actual consent. Efficacious grace Grace that actually brings about its intended saving effect. Thomist, Molinist, Augustinian, and Reformed uses differ. Irresistible grace Common Reformed name for effectual calling that renews the will and infallibly results in willing faith; not normally external coercion. Resistible grace Grace that a person can reject. The claim must specify the kind or stage of grace. Regeneration New birth or divine renewal giving spiritual life. Traditions relate it differently to faith, baptism, justification, and conversion. Monergism The claim that God alone accomplishes regeneration/conversion in the defining salvific sense. Lutheran and Reformed versions differ. Synergism Real human cooperation with indispensable divine grace. It does not mean equal causal shares or unaided merit. Justification God's act of making or declaring sinners righteous. Protestant traditions emphasize forensic imputation; Catholic and Orthodox accounts integrate forgiveness and transformative participation in different ways. Sanctification Growth or consecration in holiness by the Spirit, including transformed desire, virtue, action, and communion with God. Perseverance Continuance in saving faith to the end. Reformed doctrine grounds certain perseverance in preservation; other traditions make final apostasy possible. Apostasy Final abandonment or repudiation of faith and saving communion, distinguished from temporary doubt or serious sin followed by restoration. Theosis Participation by grace in divine life—becoming by grace what God is by nature without identity of essence—central in Eastern Christian soteriology. Historical schools and controversies Pelagianism A cluster of early-fifth-century positions contested by Augustine concerning sin, grace, and ability. The label should not be used for every synergistic view. Semi-Pelagianism A later label for positions assigning the beginning of faith to unaided will while requiring grace for progress. Its application to Cassian is disputed. Augustinianism Traditions drawing especially on Augustine's mature doctrines of original sin, grace, election, and perseverance; Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed receptions are not identical. Thomism The theological/philosophical school interpreting Thomas Aquinas, including real secondary causation, grace, and predestination. It contains internal debates. Bañezianism A Thomist school associated with Domingo Báñez that stresses physical premotion and intrinsically efficacious grace while defending voluntary action. Molinism The school derived from Luis de Molina that uses middle knowledge to coordinate providence, predestination, grace, and libertarian creaturely freedom. Arminianism A tradition deriving from Jacobus Arminius and later developments that affirms inability without grace, resistible enabling grace, and conditional election. Wesleyanism The Arminian tradition shaped by John Wesley, emphasizing universal prevenient grace, new birth, assurance, sanctification/perfect love, and possible apostasy. Maximus on willing Natural will In Maximus, the rational appetite or capacity for the good belonging to human nature. Christ has a complete human natural will. Gnomic will In Maximus's mature usage, a deliberative mode of willing associated with uncertainty and a person's manner of using natural powers. It is not simply a separate faculty, and attributing it to Christ is rejected. See also Dimensions · Grace and Salvation · Foreknowledge and Predestination · Common Confusions

docs.text: Grace and Salvation Christian traditions commonly affirm real human willing, the damage of sin, and the necessity of grace. Their disagreements concern spiritual ability, the mode and efficacy of grace, conversion, election, and perseverance—not whether grace matters. Ordinary agency is not saving ability. Someone may deliberate, keep civic order, and make voluntary choices while lacking the unaided capacity to initiate saving faith. Sin and spiritual ability Original sin in Western traditions and ancestral sin in much Eastern language name humanity's solidarity with Adam and the resulting corruption, mortality, and disorder. They are not interchangeable formulas: traditions differ about inherited guilt, deprivation, and healing. Total inability is the narrower claim that fallen people cannot turn to God savingly by their natural powers; it does not mean inability to perform any socially good act. Pelagianism The Pelagian controversy of the early fifth century concerned sin, infant baptism, grace, and whether the human will could fulfill God's commands without the interior gift of grace as Augustine understood it. Pelagius's own views, those of associates such as Caelestius and Julian, and later polemical “Pelagianism” should be distinguished. The term should not be used as a generic insult for strong accounts of choice. Semi-Pelagianism “Semi-Pelagianism” is a later label for positions associated with certain fifth- and sixth-century southern Gallic debates, especially the claim that the initial movement toward faith can arise from unaided human will even though subsequent grace is necessary. The Second Council of Orange (529) rejected an unaided beginning of faith. John Cassian's precise relation to the label remains disputed. Synergism as such is not Semi-Pelagianism , because synergistic traditions can affirm that grace initiates and enables every saving response. Monergism Monergism means that God alone accomplishes the regenerating or converting act in the relevant salvific sense . It does not entail that people are physically forced or that renewed people never act. Reformed accounts describe effectual calling as renewing the will so that the person comes freely and willingly. Lutheran confessions assign conversion entirely to the Holy Spirit through Word and sacrament, yet differ from Reformed theology on universal grace, election, resistance, baptism, and apostasy. Thus “monergist” is not a complete soteriology. Synergism Synergism means that God's grace is indispensable while the human person genuinely cooperates with grace . It does not mean “God does 50% and humans do 50%,” nor does cooperation earn the prior gift. Catholic, Orthodox, Arminian, Wesleyan, and many other synergistic accounts describe grace as creating, healing, or enabling the very response it calls for. Prevenient grace Prevenient grace is grace that precedes the saving response. In Arminian and especially Wesleyan theology, it addresses inability by enabling a response without ensuring that response. Wesley says fallen humanity cannot make even the first saving movement until God acts, then identifies the grace that goes before as “preventing grace” in “On Working Out Our Own Salvation” . Other traditions also speak of preceding grace without adopting the Wesleyan model. Article X of the Thirty-Nine Articles, for example, uses preventing for grace that gives the good will and working with for grace acting with it. Effectual or irresistible grace In Reformed theology the outward gospel call can be resisted, but the inward effectual call given to the elect succeeds. “Irresistible” does not normally mean that God drags a person to faith while leaving the person hostile. The Westminster Confession X describes renewal of the will and a person coming “most freely, being made willing by his grace.” Critics ask whether such renewal preserves the control required for responsibility; defenders answer that transformed desire is liberation rather than coercion. This is a philosophical dispute in addition to a doctrinal one. Resistible grace The question must identify the grace and stage involved: Catholic: grace precedes and enables; a person can resist. Thomist/Bañezian and Molinist schools explain sufficient and efficacious grace differently. Eastern Orthodox: divine initiative and human synergy are affirmed; resistance and apostasy remain possible. Lutheran: unregenerate people resist by nature, conversion is God's work alone, and grace can be rejected; this combination does not fit a simple Reformed/Arminian grid. Arminian/Wesleyan: prevenient grace enables but does not necessitate faith. Reformed: the general call is resistible; effectual calling infallibly brings willing response. Regeneration and faith Model Typical account Caution Reformed Regeneration is logically prior to and produces faith Logical priority need not imply a time gap Lutheran The Spirit creates faith through the means of grace; baptismal regeneration is integral Not reducible to a Reformed ordo salutis Arminian/Wesleyan Prevenient grace enables faith; regeneration is associated with believing union with Christ “Faith first” does not mean unaided faith Catholic Justification includes forgiveness and interior renewal; adults are moved by grace and freely assent Sacramental initiation resists a single abstract sequence Orthodox New birth, baptism, faith, repentance, and theosis belong to an ecclesial life of grace Often framed as healing and participation rather than an ordered mechanism Perseverance and apostasy Perseverance of the saints in confessional Reformed theology means God preserves the truly regenerate to the end. Preservation emphasizes God's sustaining action. Conditional security holds that continued saving participation is conditioned on persevering faith. Apostasy is final repudiation or abandonment of faith, not every serious lapse. Catholic and Orthodox accounts allow grace to be forfeited; restoration is possible through repentance. Lutheran confessions warn that believers can fall away. Wesleyan and many Pentecostal traditions teach conditional security. The Assemblies of God explicitly rejects unconditional security in its official assurance statement . Baptist traditions vary, though the Southern Baptist BF&M affirms perseverance. Yes Yes in the traditions surveyed here Does the person genuinely will and act? Yes, as renewed by grace Yes, enabled and sustained by grace Is conversion caused by God alone in the defining sense? docs.text: Christian traditions commonly affirm real human willing, the damage of sin, and the necessity of grace. Their disagreements concern spiritual ability, the mode and efficacy of grace, conversion, election, and perseverance—not whether grace matters. Ordinary agency is not saving ability. Someone may deliberate, keep civic order, and make voluntary choices while lacking the unaided capacity to initiate saving faith.

docs.text: Original sin in Western traditions and ancestral sin in much Eastern language name humanity's solidarity with Adam and the resulting corruption, mortality, and disorder. They are not interchangeable formulas: traditions differ about inherited guilt, deprivation, and healing. Total inability is the narrower claim that fallen people cannot turn to God savingly by their natural powers; it does not mean inability to perform any socially good act.

docs.text: The Pelagian controversy of the early fifth century concerned sin, infant baptism, grace, and whether the human will could fulfill God's commands without the interior gift of grace as Augustine understood it. Pelagius's own views, those of associates such as Caelestius and Julian, and later polemical “Pelagianism” should be distinguished. The term should not be used as a generic insult for strong accounts of choice.
docs.title: Pelagianism

docs.text: “Semi-Pelagianism” is a later label for positions associated with certain fifth- and sixth-century southern Gallic debates, especially the claim that the initial movement toward faith can arise from unaided human will even though subsequent grace is necessary. The Second Council of Orange (529) rejected an unaided beginning of faith. John Cassian's precise relation to the label remains disputed. Synergism as such is not Semi-Pelagianism , because synergistic traditions can affirm that grace initiates and enables every saving response.
docs.title: Semi-Pelagianism

docs.text: Monergism means that God alone accomplishes the regenerating or converting act in the relevant salvific sense . It does not entail that people are physically forced or that renewed people never act. Reformed accounts describe effectual calling as renewing the will so that the person comes freely and willingly. Lutheran confessions assign conversion entirely to the Holy Spirit through Word and sacrament, yet differ from Reformed theology on universal grace, election, resistance, baptism, and apostasy. Thus “monergist” is not a complete soteriology.
docs.title: Monergism

docs.text: Synergism means that God's grace is indispensable while the human person genuinely cooperates with grace . It does not mean “God does 50% and humans do 50%,” nor does cooperation earn the prior gift. Catholic, Orthodox, Arminian, Wesleyan, and many other synergistic accounts describe grace as creating, healing, or enabling the very response it calls for.
docs.title: Synergism

docs.text: Prevenient grace is grace that precedes the saving response. In Arminian and especially Wesleyan theology, it addresses inability by enabling a response without ensuring that response. Wesley says fallen humanity cannot make even the first saving movement until God acts, then identifies the grace that goes before as “preventing grace” in “On Working Out Our Own Salvation” . Other traditions also speak of preceding grace without adopting the Wesleyan model. Article X of the Thirty-Nine Articles, for example, uses preventing for grace that gives the good will and working with for grace acting with it.
docs.title: Prevenient grace

docs.text: In Reformed theology the outward gospel call can be resisted, but the inward effectual call given to the elect succeeds. “Irresistible” does not normally mean that God drags a person to faith while leaving the person hostile. The Westminster Confession X describes renewal of the will and a person coming “most freely, being made willing by his grace.” Critics ask whether such renewal preserves the control required for responsibility; defenders answer that transformed desire is liberation rather than coercion. This is a philosophical dispute in addition to a doctrinal one.
docs.title: Effectual or irresistible grace

docs.text: The question must identify the grace and stage involved: Catholic: grace precedes and enables; a person can resist. Thomist/Bañezian and Molinist schools explain sufficient and efficacious grace differently. Eastern Orthodox: divine initiative and human synergy are affirmed; resistance and apostasy remain possible. Lutheran: unregenerate people resist by nature, conversion is God's work alone, and grace can be rejected; this combination does not fit a simple Reformed/Arminian grid. Arminian/Wesleyan: prevenient grace enables but does not necessitate faith. Reformed: the general call is resistible; effectual calling infallibly brings willing response.

docs.text: Perseverance of the saints in confessional Reformed theology means God preserves the truly regenerate to the end. Preservation emphasizes God's sustaining action. Conditional security holds that continued saving participation is conditioned on persevering faith. Apostasy is final repudiation or abandonment of faith, not every serious lapse. Catholic and Orthodox accounts allow grace to be forfeited; restoration is possible through repentance. Lutheran confessions warn that believers can fall away. Wesleyan and many Pentecostal traditions teach conditional security. The Assemblies of God explicitly rejects unconditional security in its official assurance statement . Baptist traditions vary, though the Southern Baptist BF&M affirms perseverance.

docs.text: Moral Responsibility Moral responsibility concerns whether and how a person is answerable for action. It is related to free will, but a theory must still specify the relevant kind of control and the kind of responsibility at stake. Alternative possibilities and sourcehood The Principle of Alternative Possibilities (PAP) is commonly expressed as: a person is morally responsible for an action only if the person could have done otherwise. A different test asks whether the actual action genuinely issued from the agent. These tests can come apart. “Could have done otherwise” and “the action genuinely came from me” are not identical tests of freedom. A person under a covert failsafe might lack an alternative yet act entirely for their own reasons. Another person might face open alternatives but choose through an indeterministic process too disconnected from their agency to ground responsibility. Frankfurt-style cases In a standard case, a controller is prepared to force Jones to choose A if Jones shows any sign of choosing B. The controller never intervenes because Jones chooses A on his own. Jones appears responsible even though the failsafe ensured that B was unavailable. Harry Frankfurt used cases of this shape to challenge PAP. The cases are contested. Critics identify “flickers of freedom,” question whether the setup can exclude alternatives without assuming determinism, or deny the initial responsibility judgment. Their lasting value is to make the sourcehood/alternatives distinction explicit. The IEP overview introduces the argument and its role. Reasons-responsiveness A reasons-responsive account asks whether the mechanism that produced the action would recognize and react to a suitable pattern of reasons. It need not require an alternative at the exact instant. Questions remain about whether the mechanism is genuinely the agent's own and whether manipulation undermines that ownership. Coercion, compulsion, and constraint Coercion normally involves a threat or pressure that changes the cost of refusal. The coerced person may still intentionally choose, but responsibility can be reduced. Compulsion can refer to an overpowering internal drive or direct control that bypasses ordinary deliberation. Physical constraint prevents bodily action even if the person wills it. These categories are scalar and context-sensitive. Voluntariness is not simply the absence of all influence; reasons, character, relationships, and law ordinarily influence responsible action. Manipulation arguments Manipulation cases move gradually from overt programming to ordinary deterministic development. If responsibility is absent in the programmed case, the argument asks what non-arbitrary difference restores it later. Compatibilists answer with histories of ownership, opportunities for critical reflection, or other conditions; incompatibilists argue that the cases expose a deeper sourcehood deficit. Moral luck and ultimate responsibility Moral luck arises when factors beyond an agent's control—outcome, circumstances, constitution, or causal history—affect moral assessment. Ultimate responsibility demands that agents be responsible not only for acts but in some important way for the selves from which those acts issue. Critics argue this creates an impossible regress: one would have to choose the character by which one chooses. What kind of responsibility? Kind Central idea Relation to free will Basic desert Praise or blame is deserved simply because of the act Typically requires the strongest control Attributability The act expresses the agent's evaluative standpoint Emphasizes identification and character Accountability The agent is answerable within moral relationships Emphasizes demands, protest, and repair Consequential/practical Responses protect, deter, educate, or reconcile May survive skepticism about desert Theological language about judgment, culpability, repentance, and transformation can invoke different rows. It should not be imported into philosophical argument without clarification. Compare sin and spiritual ability and the dimensions framework . Frankfurt, “Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility” (1969), bibliographic details in the IEP overview

docs.text: Philosophical Views Contemporary philosophy distinguishes a claim about the truth of determinism from a claim about what freedom or responsibility requires. “Compatibilist” and “incompatibilist” identify positions on that relation; they do not by themselves describe a theology of grace. A map of the debate Is the relevant freedom compatible with determinism? ├── Yes: compatibilism └── No: incompatibilism ├── Freedom exists: libertarianism └── Freedom does not exist or is doubtful ├── hard determinism ├── hard incompatibilism └── free-will skepticism Libertarian free will Libertarians affirm meaningful free will and hold that it is incompatible with causal determinism. Many require alternative possibilities; source libertarians place the emphasis on the agent as the appropriate origin of action. Major families include: Agent-causal theories: the agent, not merely an event in the agent, causes a choice in a distinctive way. Event-causal theories: indeterministic relations among beliefs, desires, efforts, and decisions explain action without a special substance-causal power. Non-causal theories: a basic action or decision can be purposive without being caused by prior events. Indeterminism alone does not produce freedom. If chance simply interrupts a causal chain, it is unclear why the result belongs more fully to the agent. The luck objection therefore presses libertarians to explain enhanced control, rational explanation, and ownership—not merely openness. See also Alternative Possibilities and the SEP survey of incompatibilist theories . Compatibilism Compatibilism holds that determinism and the relevant freedom can coexist. Classical versions focus on voluntary action without external constraint: the agent does what they want to do. Contemporary versions add hierarchical identification, ownership of motives, guidance control, or reasons-responsiveness. Compatibilists need not deny every meaningful “could have done otherwise.” Some use conditional or dispositional analyses; others argue that responsibility depends primarily on how the actual sequence issued from the agent. Frankfurt-style cases motivate the latter approach. The main objections include: Manipulation: if an agent's values were engineered, acting from them may not be enough. Consequence: if the past and laws are not up to us, how can their fixed consequences be up to us? Sourcehood: does a deterministic history leave the agent sufficiently ultimate or authentic? See the SEP entry on compatibilism and Moral Responsibility . Incompatibilism Incompatibilism is the umbrella thesis that determinism excludes the relevant kind of freedom. It does not entail belief in free will: libertarians affirm freedom, whereas hard determinists and hard incompatibilists deny or doubt it. Hard determinism Hard determinists accept determinism and conclude that free will of the required kind does not exist. The position must then revise or reject practices grounded in basic desert, though it may preserve deterrence, moral education, protection, and interpersonal expectations. Hard incompatibilism Hard incompatibilists argue that neither deterministic nor indeterministic processes give agents the control needed for basic-desert responsibility. The problem is therefore deeper than determinism: an action produced by chance may be no more ultimately controlled than one fixed by prior causes. Free-will skepticism Skepticism is a broader family of views holding that strong free will is absent, incoherent, or insufficiently justified. A skeptic may remain agnostic about determinism. Skeptics differ on whether responsibility practices should be retained, reformed, or abandoned. Semi-compatibilism Semi-compatibilism, associated especially with John Martin Fischer, holds that moral responsibility may be compatible with determinism even if the freedom to do otherwise is not. The proposal separates regulative control (access to alternatives) from guidance control (the actual action issuing through the agent's own suitably reasons-responsive mechanism). Comparison Position Determinism compatible with freedom? Affirms free will? Alternatives required? Recurring challenge Libertarianism No Yes Usually, though source accounts vary Luck, randomness, and control Compatibilism Yes Yes Not necessarily Manipulation and sourcehood Hard determinism No No No Reconstructing responsibility Hard incompatibilism No adequate freedom either way Usually no No Agency and practical life without desert Free-will skepticism Doubtful or irrelevant No or agnostic No Scope of revision to moral practices Semi-compatibilism Responsibility may be Varies No for responsibility Ground of guidance control “Free will?” and “moral responsibility?” remain distinguishable questions. The SEP discussion of incompatibilist arguments explicitly cautions against collapsing them. Reformed Assessment Libertarianism's strongest contribution is its insistence on creaturely sourcehood and genuine alternatives. From a confessional Reformed perspective, its principal costs are that indeterminacy does not itself explain enhanced control, alternative possibilities may not be necessary for responsibility, and undetermined creaturely decisions fit comprehensive providence less naturally. Compatibilism better supports voluntary responsibility under providence, but must answer manipulation and ultimate-sourcehood objections. Hard determinism and skepticism are also rejected because they thin responsible personal agency rather than locating it within purposeful divine and secondary causation. See A Reformed Evaluation of Free Will for the full, intentionally confessional argument.
