docs.text: A Reformed Evaluation of Free Will This page evaluates the major free-will and grace traditions from a confessional Reformed perspective. Historical descriptions elsewhere in this wiki remain descriptive; the analysis here is intentionally theological and evaluative. The Reformed account is presented here as the strongest synthesis because it preserves comprehensive divine sovereignty, radical dependence on grace, meaningful human voluntariness and responsibility, unconditional election, effectual calling, and perseverance without making salvation finally depend on an autonomous human decision. This is a cumulative argument, not a claim that Reformed theology has no hard questions. Its governing comparison is explanatory cost : what must each model affirm, qualify, or leave unresolved in order to hold together its account of providence, agency, sin, grace, and final salvation? Criteria for Evaluation These are confessional Reformed theological criteria , not religiously neutral axioms. A reader who rejects the Reformed doctrine of Scripture, providence, or sin will predictably rank the models differently. Does the position preserve the biblical depiction of God's comprehensive sovereignty? Does it take fallen human inability seriously? Does it make divine grace genuinely decisive in salvation? Does it preserve meaningful human responsibility? Does it distinguish voluntariness from libertarian indeterminacy? Does it adequately explain election and predestination? Does it account for texts in which divine ordination and human intention operate simultaneously? Does it avoid making the decisive difference between believer and unbeliever rest finally in autonomous self-determination? Does it give a coherent relation among regeneration, faith, and perseverance? Does it maintain God's holiness while affirming comprehensive providence? Does it explain the relevant texts with fewer ad hoc qualifications than competing systems? Is its philosophical account of agency internally coherent? The Reformed Account Comprehensive providence God does not merely observe a history constituted independently of divine purpose. God creates, sustains, concurs with, and governs creaturely causes, while those creatures remain real secondary causes. Westminster Confession V therefore joins meticulous providence to creaturely contingency and denies that God is the author or approver of sin; Belgic Confession 13 makes the same holiness qualification. Genesis 50:20, Isaiah 10, Acts 2:23, and Acts 4:27–28 display the characteristic pattern: the same event may be ordained by God for a holy purpose and performed by human agents for sinful purposes . Divine and creaturely intentions are concurrent, but they are neither morally identical nor rival causes on the same level. Human voluntariness Reformed theology does not require a free action to be causally undetermined. It requires the action to proceed voluntarily from the person's own desires, intentions, character, and reasoning rather than from external coercion. Determination and coercion are therefore different claims. The remaining philosophical dispute is whether voluntariness, ownership, and reasons-responsiveness provide enough sourcehood for moral desert. Fallen inability The account distinguishes three things: possession of ordinary human faculties; voluntary deliberation and choice; moral and spiritual ability to love God rightly. Fallen people retain mind and will, yet do not generate saving faith from an unrenewed disposition. Belgic Confession 14 and Westminster Confession IX therefore deny saving ability without denying human agency. Jonathan Edwards's natural/moral inability distinction is a later analytical expression of this pattern, not the definition of every Reformed confession. Effectual grace fallen sinner ↓ effectual calling / regeneration ↓ renewed disposition ↓ willing faith and repentance God does not force an unwilling believer to believe; God renews the heart so that the person willingly comes. Westminster Confession X , Westminster Larger Catechism 67 , and Canons of Dort III/IV.11–14 make grace causally productive of both the ability and act of faith. The regenerated person is active in believing; monergism identifies the source of the renewing act, not the absence of the human response. Unconditional election Election rests on God's gracious purpose rather than foreseen merit or autonomous faith. Faith is the ordained effect and instrument of salvation, not the independent condition that explains why one person enters the elect company. The Canons of Dort I and Belgic Confession 16 state this while also locating judgment in human sin. Perseverance Final salvation rests on divine preservation, exercised through faith, warning, prayer, sacrament, discipline, and other appointed means. Perseverance is not confidence in the permanence of an autonomous choice. Westminster Confession XVII and Canons of Dort V also acknowledge serious falls, disrupted assurance, and the real efficacy of warnings. A Cumulative Case comprehensive providence + radical fallen inability + decisive divine grace + voluntary human agency + unconditional election + effectual calling + perseverance = a unified Reformed account The argument does not depend on Calvin's authority alone. Its force is the proposed mutual support among these doctrines: providence supplies a framework for concurrent agency; inability establishes the need for causally effective grace; effectual calling explains willing faith; election identifies grace's gracious source; and preservation carries the same divine initiative to completion. A Biblical Case with Exegetical Hinges The passages below are not detached proof texts. Each is presented with a serious alternative and the point at which interpretation turns. Genesis 50:20; Isaiah 10; Acts 2:23; Acts 4:27–28 Reformed reading Joseph's brothers intend evil while God intends the same action for good. Assyria acts arrogantly while serving a divine purpose it does not share. Jesus is crucified by culpable agents according to God's plan, and Acts 4 describes their acts as predestined. Together these passages supply a pattern of divine-human concurrence. Major alternative reading A libertarian providential reading can treat these as specially governed redemptive events: God foreknows, permits, limits, and incorporates wicked choices without causally determining every intention. Exceptional predetermination need not establish a general compatibilist account. Exegetical hinge The dispute turns on whether the texts attribute only foreknown permission and subsequent use to God, or a prior intention and appointment encompassing the creaturely event; it also turns on how representative these events are of providence generally. Reformed assessment The verbs of intention, plan, and predestination make bare permission too thin, while the texts' direct blame of human agents excludes fatalism. The concurrence reading therefore explains both claims without making divine purpose and creaturely culpability compete. Ezekiel 36:26–27 and John 6:37–45 Reformed reading God removes the heart of stone, gives a new heart, and causes covenant obedience; those given by the Father come to the Son, and the Father's drawing succeeds in resurrection on the last day. Renewal explains the willing response rather than merely restoring neutrality. Major alternative reading Arminian and Wesleyan readings understand enabling grace as prior and indispensable but resistible. Ezekiel may describe corporate covenant restoration, while John 6 may describe drawing through revelation that can be refused and must be read alongside broader invitations. Exegetical hinge The decisive questions are whether heart-renewal causes the faithful response, whether the giving and drawing in John 6 are coextensive with those who come and are raised, and how the immediate audience and wider canonical invitations determine scope. Reformed assessment The promised transformation and the linked sequence of giving, coming, and raising fit effectual renewal more directly than a universally restored but indeterminate capacity. The alternative preserves universal enablement, but must supply that universality from other texts and systematic inference. Romans 8:28–30; Romans 9; Ephesians 1–2; Acts 13:48 Reformed reading God's purpose links foreknowledge, predestination, calling, justification, and glorification; Romans 9 grounds mercy in God's call rather than willing or running; Ephesians locates election before creation and faith within grace; Acts relates appointment to life and belief. Election is particular, unconditional, and causally integrated with calling and faith. Major alternative reading Conditional and corporate readings understand election primarily in Christ and identify the elect body through faith. “Foreknown” may name foreseen believers or covenant relationship; Romans 9 may focus on historical vocation and the constitution of God's people rather than an exhaustive order of individual salvation. Arminius's Declaration of Sentiments is an important primary example of a Christ-centered, conditional construction. Exegetical hinge Interpretation turns on the objects of foreknowledge and election, the role of individuals within the corporate argument, whether calling produces the saving response, and whether Paul's “not by works” contrast also excludes foreseen faith as election's ground. Reformed assessment No single verse settles every later question, but the cumulative order from purpose through calling to faith is more naturally causal than reactive. Corporate election is real, yet does not by itself explain why particular people are savingly incorporated. 1 Timothy 2:1–6 and 2 Peter 3:8–10 Reformed reading These texts ground indiscriminate prayer and gospel proclamation and reveal God's real benevolence. Reformed interpreters variously understand “all” as all kinds of people, distinguish God's preceptive or revealed will from the decree, and read 2 Peter's patience in relation to its addressed “beloved.” No faithful Reformed reading may turn the invitations into insincere language. Major alternative reading Arminian, Wesleyan, Lutheran, Catholic, and Orthodox readers commonly take the passages as affirming God's saving desire for every individual and therefore as pressure against a decree of particular effectual grace. Exegetical hinge The dispute turns on the scope of “all,” the addressees of each letter, whether Scripture may speak of divine will in more than one sense, and how these texts relate canonically to particular-election passages. Reformed assessment The universal reading is a serious objection, not a verbal mistake. Yet a universal saving desire does not by itself establish universal libertarian enablement or settle how God's revealed compassion relates to redemptive purpose. The Reformed distinctions are defensible when they arise from context and the whole canon rather than being invoked only to protect a system. Hebrews 6:4–12 and Hebrews 10:19–39 Reformed reading The warnings address the covenant community and are means by which God preserves believers. Reformed interpreters differ over the precise status of those described, but commonly distinguish profound participation in covenant blessings from the regenerating union that certainly perseveres. Major alternative reading Lutheran, Wesleyan, Catholic, and Orthodox readings can take the descriptions as referring to genuine believers who may finally repudiate grace. The Formula of Concord XI and Wesley's “On Working Out Our Own Salvation” represent traditions in which warning and possible apostasy belong together. Exegetical hinge The questions are whether the experiential descriptions entail regeneration, how the agricultural analogy in Hebrews 6 functions, and whether a divinely effective warning can describe a danger that God uses to prevent among the elect. Reformed assessment The apostasy reading gives the warning language its most immediate force. Reformed perseverance remains coherent, however, if warnings are real instruments rather than predictions that the regenerate will finally fall. The status of the apostates remains one of the framework's most disputed exegetical questions. Why Libertarian Freedom Is Weaker Libertarian freedom seeks to preserve genuine alternatives and strong creaturely sourcehood. It argues that, for at least some morally significant actions, the agent must be able to choose otherwise under the same relevant conditions. Agent-causal, event-causal, and non-causal versions should not be collapsed. Weakness 1: indeterminacy does not explain control The luck objection asks: what makes an undetermined choice more genuinely mine rather than merely less determined? Libertarian theories answer with agent causation, purposive effort, or indeterministic reasons-sensitive processes; the SEP survey treats these as substantive replies. Yet every version still owes an account of why the actual outcome expresses enhanced control when the same prior conditions leave another outcome open. Indeterminacy is not identical to randomness, but it is not yet an explanation of ownership. Weakness 2: alternatives may not be necessary for responsibility Frankfurt-style cases, voluntariness, actual-sequence sourcehood, and reasons-responsiveness make it plausible that responsibility tracks what a person knowingly intends and loves, even when a contrary option is unavailable. The cases remain disputed, as the SEP discussion of compatibilism notes, but libertarianism cannot simply assume the Principle of Alternative Possibilities. Weakness 3: strong libertarianism raises a providence cost If decisive creaturely choices are categorically undetermined by divine providence, the Reformed account judges them difficult to integrate with the scriptural concurrence pattern. Molinism offers world-selection through middle knowledge, but transfers the cost to pre-decretal counterfactuals and their grounding. Weakness 4: libertarianism does not solve spiritual inability Even if libertarian agency describes some ordinary choices, it does not establish that fallen people can love God savingly. A further doctrine of enabling grace is still required. Reformed conclusion: libertarianism incurs substantial metaphysical costs without being necessary to explain moral responsibility or biblical divine-human concurrence. Why the Arminian Solution Is Weaker Arminian theology is not Pelagianism. Arminius denies saving ability apart from grace; grace precedes, accompanies, and sustains response, remains resistible, and election is commonly related to foreknown faith. His own account of final apostasy was cautious, while later Remonstrants developed it further. See Arminius's “Grace and Free Will” and the 1610 Remonstrance . Weakness 1: the decisive-difference problem If two equally fallen sinners receive genuinely sufficient enabling grace, and one believes while the other resists, what finally explains the difference? The Arminian reply is that neither response is ungraced, faith merits nothing, and a personal response need not compete with grace. The Reformed concern remains causal rather than meritorious: if grace supplies equal sufficient ability while the undetermined assent differentiates the outcomes, grace is necessary but not finally decisive at the point of difference. Weakness 2: election can appear reactive Conditional election protects the priority of Christ and excludes merit. Yet when foreseen faith is election's condition, election recognizes the successful response rather than explaining why saving grace produces it. Weakness 3: universal enabling grace bears a large exegetical burden Universal prevenient or enabling grace is systematically coherent, but the Reformed reading disputes that Scripture clearly teaches a universal restoration of libertarian saving ability. The doctrine often functions as the bridge between universal invitation, total inability, and resistible faith; each of those concerns is textually motivated, but the bridge itself requires cumulative inference. Weakness 4: perseverance becomes contingent Where final apostasy is possible, final salvation depends in part on continued non-resistance. Arminianism remains grace-centered, but from the Reformed standpoint it does not make grace decisive at the final explanatory point. Why the Wesleyan Solution Is Weaker Wesleyanism strongly affirms total inability apart from grace, universal prevenient grace, resistible response, assurance, sanctification, and commonly conditional security. The United Methodist doctrinal standards and Wesley's sermons should control its representation. Weakness 1: prevenient grace carries major explanatory weight Universal prevenient grace must both answer inability and restore response without determining it. The Reformed question is whether this universal restoration is directly taught or is principally a systematic inference joining universal invitation to libertarian response. Weakness 2: the decisive-difference problem remains If grace restores genuine saving ability to all, the differing response finally distinguishes belief from unbelief. Wesleyans answer that every good impulse remains graced and faith is not meritorious; the Reformed critique is again about explanatory efficacy, not earning. Weakness 3: apostasy complicates perseverance and assurance Wesleyan assurance is real and Spirit-given. Nevertheless, if a regenerate person may finally fall, present assurance does not include the same ground of certain divine preservation affirmed at Dort. Strength acknowledged Wesleyanism preserves the priority of grace, universal gospel invitation, meaningful response, and sustained attention to holy love. The Reformed account judges effectual grace stronger because the same grace that initiates renewal also explains faith and final perseverance. Why Catholic Accounts Are Weaker from a Reformed Perspective Roman Catholicism is not one metaphysical theory. It rejects Pelagianism, affirms divine initiative and necessary grace, and contains sophisticated accounts of divine causation. Thomist/Bañezian approaches, Molinism, and the broader Catholic doctrine of grace must be distinguished. Weakness 1: the confessional disagreement over justification The Catechism on grace and justification and Trent, Session VI describe initial justification as gratuitous while including interior renewal, free grace-enabled cooperation, sacramental life, and the possibility of grace-enabled merit. The Reformed confessions distinguish justification from sanctification and ground acceptance in Christ's imputed righteousness received through faith alone. The central weakness, under Reformed criteria, is not an absence of grace but a soteriology that does not preserve sola gratia and justification in the same confessional sense. Weakness 2: Molinism depends on controversial middle knowledge Molinism combines libertarian freedom and meticulous providence through God's pre-decretal knowledge of true counterfactuals of creaturely freedom. Its explanatory cost is the grounding question: what makes those counterfactuals true independently of God's decree and the creature's actual decision? The SEP providence survey presents the proposal and major objections. Weakness 3: Thomism nears strong divine causality but differs in soteriology Thomist/Bañezian motion is metaphysically closer to strong divine causation than popular “Catholic free will” summaries suggest. The deeper Reformed disagreements concern justification, merit, sacramental theology, perseverance, and ecclesiology. Thomism is therefore neither Molinism nor Reformed theology. Reformed conclusion: Catholic theology has formidable metaphysical resources, but it does not preserve the same confessional account of sola gratia and justification. Why the Orthodox Synergistic Account Is Weaker Eastern Orthodoxy treats grace as indispensable divine life and action, freedom as healed, salvation as participation and theosis, and synergy as real grace-sustained cooperation—not a 50/50 transaction. John of Damascus and the Orthodox Church in America provide representative sources, though Orthodoxy has no single modern analytic theory. Weakness 1: synergy leaves the decisive-response question open The relational and participatory model explains what salvation is, but if grace may finally be resisted, the same question recurs: what ultimately differentiates cooperation from resistance? Saying that the person truly participates protects agency but does not yet identify why grace reaches its saving effect in one case. Weakness 2: anthropology of the Fall differs Orthodox sources commonly emphasize inherited mortality and corruption rather than inherited guilt and Reformed moral inability. This is neither Pelagianism nor denial of grace. From the Reformed framework, however, it understates the depth of inability expressed in John 6, Romans 8, and Ephesians 2 and therefore reduces the need for effectual renewal. Weakness 3: election texts carry less causal weight Orthodox readings commonly integrate election with foreknowledge, Christ, and the divine desire to save without giving unconditional individual election the Reformed causal role. Reformed readers judge Romans 8–9, Ephesians 1, and Acts 13:48 more naturally explained by particular election and effectual calling. Weakness 4: categories are weighted differently The absence of a Reformed ordo salutis is not by itself an intellectual defect; Orthodoxy organizes salvation around participation, sacrament, and theosis. The narrower assessment is that, under the stated Reformed criteria, the Orthodox model gives less explanatory force to unconditional election and effectual calling. Why Lutheranism Comes Close but Remains Weaker Confessional Lutheranism strongly affirms bondage of the fallen will, monergistic conversion through Word and sacrament, universal grace, and rejection of Pelagian cooperation. The Formula of Concord II says conversion is wholly the Spirit's work, while Lutheran doctrine also affirms resistance and possible apostasy. Tension 1: resistible grace plus monergistic conversion If conversion is wholly God's work, why does the same grace result in conversion in one case and final resistance in another? Lutheran theology often refuses to infer beyond what it judges Scripture has revealed and locates blame wholly in the resistor; appeal to mystery is not irrationality. Reformed theology nevertheless considers unconditional election and effectual calling a more systematic resolution because divine grace explains the positive difference. Tension 2: apostasy Possible loss of regeneration means the grace that monergistically creates faith does not ensure completion. Within the Reformed framework, preservation is more consistent with effectual renewal, while warnings remain divinely appointed means. Tension 3: election and non-election Formula of Concord XI teaches election to salvation in Christ and refuses a symmetrical decree, tracing condemnation to sin and resistance. Reformed confessions agree on asymmetrical culpability but integrate non-election within a more comprehensive decree. The Reformed gain is systematic integration; its added burden is the author-of-sin objection. Reformed conclusion: Lutheranism is among the closest alternatives, but it is less systematic where monergistic grace, resistibility, election, and apostasy intersect. Why Hard Determinism and Free-Will Skepticism Are Weaker Reformed theology is not “secular hard determinism plus God.” It affirms personal agency, rational deliberation, voluntariness, moral responsibility, purposeful providence, and layered primary and secondary causation. Hard determinism and strong responsibility skepticism gain causal simplicity at the cost of a sufficiently rich account of responsible personal agency. Skeptical models can preserve forward-looking protection and formation, but revision of basic-desert responsibility is precisely what Reformed moral theology rejects. See the SEP overview of responsibility skepticism . A Brief Reformed Assessment of Open Theism Open theism protects providential responsiveness by holding that some future free acts are not yet definite truths. From the Reformed perspective, this adds greater costs than classical Arminianism: exhaustive definite foreknowledge, the specificity of prophecy, and confidence in comprehensive providence all require revision. Open theists affirm omniscience as knowledge of reality exactly as it is, so “God guesses” is a caricature; the disagreement concerns whether future free actions are definite objects of knowledge. See the SEP foreknowledge survey . Comparative Explanatory Costs View Main strength Principal weakness from a Reformed perspective Libertarianism Strong alternatives and creaturely sourcehood Indeterminacy does not itself secure control and fits comprehensive providence less naturally Arminianism Universal invitation, prior grace, and resistible response Enabling grace does not finally explain why one person believes Wesleyanism Developed universal prevenient grace and sanctification Prevenient grace carries large exegetical and explanatory weight Molinism Sophisticated reconciliation of providence and libertarian freedom Grounding and providence problems surround middle knowledge Catholic Thomism Strong divine causality and secondary causes Different doctrine of justification and unresolved internal freedom debates Eastern Orthodox synergy Relational, participatory account of salvation Less compatible with Reformed readings of inability, election, and effectual calling Lutheranism Monergistic conversion and strong means-of-grace theology Tension among monergism, resistibility, election, and apostasy Hard determinism / skepticism Strong causal or revisionary critique Thin account of moral responsibility and theological agency Open theism Strong account of responsive divine-human relations Revises exhaustive definite foreknowledge and weakens providential certainty Reformed compatibilism Integrates providence, grace, and responsibility Must answer author-of-sin, evil, manipulation, and ultimate-sourcehood objections Why the Reformed Model Is Stronger Grace is decisive rather than merely enabling. God's regenerating grace, not an autonomous difference in response, explains saving faith. Providence is comprehensive. One concurrence framework covers ordinary causes, sinful acts, the crucifixion, conversion, and perseverance. Human willing remains real. Determination is not coercion; people deliberate and act from their own reasons and loves. Fallen inability is treated consistently. Regeneration does more than return a sinner to metaphysical neutrality; it renews the disposition. Election is integrated with grace. Election explains why grace reaches saving effect rather than recognizing a future response. Perseverance is grounded in divine preservation. The God who begins renewal completes it through appointed means. Libertarian metaphysics is unnecessary. Voluntariness, actual-sequence sourcehood, and reasons-responsiveness do the required agency work with fewer metaphysical commitments. Scripture contains strong examples of concurrent agency. Joseph and his brothers, Assyria, and the crucifixion join divine purpose to responsible creaturely intention without moral equivalence. From a confessional Reformed standpoint, the principal advantage is not one isolated doctrine, but the way providence, sin, grace, election, voluntary agency, and perseverance mutually reinforce one another. The Hardest Questions for the Reformed Position God and the ordination of evil If every event falls within providence, why is God not the author of sin? Reformed confessions distinguish God's holy ordination and concurrence from the creature's defective intention, deny that divine causation is morally symmetrical with creaturely causation, and invoke secondary causes. That is a coherent distinction, but the problem of evil demands more than repeating it: the account must show that God has morally sufficient purposes and does not inject evil motives into agents. Ultimate sourcehood If a person's character and desires are ultimately within a determined order, is the person a sufficient source for basic desert? Compatibilist replies appeal to ownership, rational agency, and action flowing from the person's own evaluative standpoint. Manipulation arguments press whether that source is deep enough. This is probably the strongest philosophical objection to the model. Universal-saving-will passages First Timothy 2 and 2 Peter 3 appear to express a broad divine desire to save. Reformed distinctions among decree, precept, benevolence, and all kinds of people must be contextually demonstrated rather than used as escape clauses. The universal readings remain important evidence against particular election. Love and effectual grace Does transforming desire preserve meaningful relational freedom, or would love require the live possibility of final refusal? The Reformed reply is that healed love can be most free when it is most fully inclined to the good; God's work establishes willing communion rather than bypassing it. A libertarian will dispute whether transformed willingness is enough. These objections are serious, but need not be fatal if concurrent agency is coherent, voluntariness grounds responsibility, and the scriptural case for effectual grace and election is cumulative. The comparative claim is that rival systems face greater or less manageable costs—not that Reformed theology has no mysteries. Sources and Further Study Reformed primary and confessional sources Westminster Confession of Faith; Larger and Shorter Catechisms , especially WCF III, V, IX–X, XVII; WLC 67; WSC 20, 30–32 Canons of Dort , especially I, III/IV, and V Heidelberg Catechism , especially questions 1, 8, 20–21, 53–54, and 60–64 Belgic Confession , especially articles 13–16 and 22–24 Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion , especially II.2–5 and III.21–24 Edwards, Freedom of the Will Francis Turretin, Institutes of Elenctic Theology , topics 4, 9, 10, and 15 (consult a scholarly edition) Herman Bavinck, Reformed Dogmatics , volumes 2–4 (consult a scholarly edition) Augustine is an important antecedent, especially On Grace and Free Will and On the Gift of Perseverance , but he is not “a Calvinist before Calvin.” Luther's account of bondage is also important while Lutheran and Reformed confessions remain distinct. Sources representing alternatives Arminian: Arminius, Declaration of Sentiments and “Grace and Free Will” ; 1610 Remonstrance Wesleyan: Wesley, “On Working Out Our Own Salvation” and “Free Grace” ; United Methodist doctrinal standards Lutheran: Formula of Concord II and XI Roman Catholic: Catechism on grace and justification ; Council of Trent, Session VI ; Aquinas, Summa theologiae I q.23, I q.83, I–II qq.109–114 Eastern Orthodox: John of Damascus, Exact Exposition II.22–30 ; Orthodox Church in America, The Orthodox Faith and “Salvation Is Indeed by Grace” Philosophy: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy on compatibilism , incompatibilist theories , divine providence , and foreknowledge For neutral historical descriptions, return to Philosophical Views , Grace and Salvation , Christian Traditions , and the Comparison Matrix . Conclusion The competing traditions preserve genuine biblical and theological concerns, especially the seriousness of human response, the universality of gospel proclamation, and relational language about grace. From a confessional Reformed perspective, however, they generally preserve these concerns at a greater explanatory cost: grace becomes enabling rather than finally decisive, providence becomes less comprehensive, election becomes conditioned or less causally central, or perseverance becomes contingent on continued human response. The Reformed account is therefore judged strongest because it makes grace finally decisive, preserves comprehensive providence and voluntary responsibility, takes fallen inability seriously, grounds election in God's purpose, treats regeneration as productive of faith, grounds perseverance in divine preservation, avoids requiring libertarian indeterminacy, and offers a unified account of divine and human agency. That conclusion remains conditional on sustaining its compatibilist account of responsibility and its distinction between divine ordination and divine moral approval of evil. This is intentionally a Reformed conclusion.

docs.text: Election rests on God's gracious purpose rather than foreseen merit or autonomous faith. Faith is the ordained effect and instrument of salvation, not the independent condition that explains why one person enters the elect company. The Canons of Dort I and Belgic Confession 16 state this while also locating judgment in human sin.
docs.title: Unconditional election

docs.text: Final salvation rests on divine preservation, exercised through faith, warning, prayer, sacrament, discipline, and other appointed means. Perseverance is not confidence in the permanence of an autonomous choice. Westminster Confession XVII and Canons of Dort V also acknowledge serious falls, disrupted assurance, and the real efficacy of warnings.
docs.title: Perseverance

docs.text: comprehensive providence + radical fallen inability + decisive divine grace + voluntary human agency + unconditional election + effectual calling + perseverance = a unified Reformed account The argument does not depend on Calvin's authority alone. Its force is the proposed mutual support among these doctrines: providence supplies a framework for concurrent agency; inability establishes the need for causally effective grace; effectual calling explains willing faith; election identifies grace's gracious source; and preservation carries the same divine initiative to completion.
docs.title: A Cumulative Case

docs.text: The passages below are not detached proof texts. Each is presented with a serious alternative and the point at which interpretation turns.
docs.title: A Biblical Case with Exegetical Hinges

docs.text: Joseph's brothers intend evil while God intends the same action for good. Assyria acts arrogantly while serving a divine purpose it does not share. Jesus is crucified by culpable agents according to God's plan, and Acts 4 describes their acts as predestined. Together these passages supply a pattern of divine-human concurrence.
docs.title: Reformed reading

docs.text: A libertarian providential reading can treat these as specially governed redemptive events: God foreknows, permits, limits, and incorporates wicked choices without causally determining every intention. Exceptional predetermination need not establish a general compatibilist account.
docs.title: Major alternative reading

docs.text: The dispute turns on whether the texts attribute only foreknown permission and subsequent use to God, or a prior intention and appointment encompassing the creaturely event; it also turns on how representative these events are of providence generally.
docs.title: Exegetical hinge

docs.text: The verbs of intention, plan, and predestination make bare permission too thin, while the texts' direct blame of human agents excludes fatalism. The concurrence reading therefore explains both claims without making divine purpose and creaturely culpability compete.
docs.title: Reformed assessment

docs.text: God removes the heart of stone, gives a new heart, and causes covenant obedience; those given by the Father come to the Son, and the Father's drawing succeeds in resurrection on the last day. Renewal explains the willing response rather than merely restoring neutrality.
docs.title: Reformed reading

docs.text: Arminian and Wesleyan readings understand enabling grace as prior and indispensable but resistible. Ezekiel may describe corporate covenant restoration, while John 6 may describe drawing through revelation that can be refused and must be read alongside broader invitations.
docs.title: Major alternative reading

docs.text: The decisive questions are whether heart-renewal causes the faithful response, whether the giving and drawing in John 6 are coextensive with those who come and are raised, and how the immediate audience and wider canonical invitations determine scope.
docs.title: Exegetical hinge

docs.text: The promised transformation and the linked sequence of giving, coming, and raising fit effectual renewal more directly than a universally restored but indeterminate capacity. The alternative preserves universal enablement, but must supply that universality from other texts and systematic inference.
docs.title: Reformed assessment

docs.text: God's purpose links foreknowledge, predestination, calling, justification, and glorification; Romans 9 grounds mercy in God's call rather than willing or running; Ephesians locates election before creation and faith within grace; Acts relates appointment to life and belief. Election is particular, unconditional, and causally integrated with calling and faith.
docs.title: Reformed reading

docs.text: Conditional and corporate readings understand election primarily in Christ and identify the elect body through faith. “Foreknown” may name foreseen believers or covenant relationship; Romans 9 may focus on historical vocation and the constitution of God's people rather than an exhaustive order of individual salvation. Arminius's Declaration of Sentiments is an important primary example of a Christ-centered, conditional construction.
docs.title: Major alternative reading

docs.text: Interpretation turns on the objects of foreknowledge and election, the role of individuals within the corporate argument, whether calling produces the saving response, and whether Paul's “not by works” contrast also excludes foreseen faith as election's ground.
docs.title: Exegetical hinge

docs.text: No single verse settles every later question, but the cumulative order from purpose through calling to faith is more naturally causal than reactive. Corporate election is real, yet does not by itself explain why particular people are savingly incorporated.
docs.title: Reformed assessment

docs.text: These texts ground indiscriminate prayer and gospel proclamation and reveal God's real benevolence. Reformed interpreters variously understand “all” as all kinds of people, distinguish God's preceptive or revealed will from the decree, and read 2 Peter's patience in relation to its addressed “beloved.” No faithful Reformed reading may turn the invitations into insincere language.
docs.title: Reformed reading

docs.text: Arminian, Wesleyan, Lutheran, Catholic, and Orthodox readers commonly take the passages as affirming God's saving desire for every individual and therefore as pressure against a decree of particular effectual grace.
docs.title: Major alternative reading

docs.text: The dispute turns on the scope of “all,” the addressees of each letter, whether Scripture may speak of divine will in more than one sense, and how these texts relate canonically to particular-election passages.
docs.title: Exegetical hinge

docs.text: The universal reading is a serious objection, not a verbal mistake. Yet a universal saving desire does not by itself establish universal libertarian enablement or settle how God's revealed compassion relates to redemptive purpose. The Reformed distinctions are defensible when they arise from context and the whole canon rather than being invoked only to protect a system.
docs.title: Reformed assessment

docs.text: The warnings address the covenant community and are means by which God preserves believers. Reformed interpreters differ over the precise status of those described, but commonly distinguish profound participation in covenant blessings from the regenerating union that certainly perseveres.
docs.title: Reformed reading

docs.text: Lutheran, Wesleyan, Catholic, and Orthodox readings can take the descriptions as referring to genuine believers who may finally repudiate grace. The Formula of Concord XI and Wesley's “On Working Out Our Own Salvation” represent traditions in which warning and possible apostasy belong together.
docs.title: Major alternative reading

docs.text: The questions are whether the experiential descriptions entail regeneration, how the agricultural analogy in Hebrews 6 functions, and whether a divinely effective warning can describe a danger that God uses to prevent among the elect.
docs.title: Exegetical hinge

docs.text: The apostasy reading gives the warning language its most immediate force. Reformed perseverance remains coherent, however, if warnings are real instruments rather than predictions that the regenerate will finally fall. The status of the apostates remains one of the framework's most disputed exegetical questions.
docs.title: Reformed assessment

docs.text: Libertarian freedom seeks to preserve genuine alternatives and strong creaturely sourcehood. It argues that, for at least some morally significant actions, the agent must be able to choose otherwise under the same relevant conditions. Agent-causal, event-causal, and non-causal versions should not be collapsed.
docs.title: Why Libertarian Freedom Is Weaker

docs.text: The luck objection asks: what makes an undetermined choice more genuinely mine rather than merely less determined? Libertarian theories answer with agent causation, purposive effort, or indeterministic reasons-sensitive processes; the SEP survey treats these as substantive replies. Yet every version still owes an account of why the actual outcome expresses enhanced control when the same prior conditions leave another outcome open. Indeterminacy is not identical to randomness, but it is not yet an explanation of ownership.
docs.title: Weakness 1: indeterminacy does not explain control

docs.text: Frankfurt-style cases, voluntariness, actual-sequence sourcehood, and reasons-responsiveness make it plausible that responsibility tracks what a person knowingly intends and loves, even when a contrary option is unavailable. The cases remain disputed, as the SEP discussion of compatibilism notes, but libertarianism cannot simply assume the Principle of Alternative Possibilities.
docs.title: Weakness 2: alternatives may not be necessary for responsibility

docs.text: If decisive creaturely choices are categorically undetermined by divine providence, the Reformed account judges them difficult to integrate with the scriptural concurrence pattern. Molinism offers world-selection through middle knowledge, but transfers the cost to pre-decretal counterfactuals and their grounding.
docs.title: Weakness 3: strong libertarianism raises a providence cost

docs.text: Even if libertarian agency describes some ordinary choices, it does not establish that fallen people can love God savingly. A further doctrine of enabling grace is still required. Reformed conclusion: libertarianism incurs substantial metaphysical costs without being necessary to explain moral responsibility or biblical divine-human concurrence.
docs.title: Weakness 4: libertarianism does not solve spiritual inability

docs.text: Arminian theology is not Pelagianism. Arminius denies saving ability apart from grace; grace precedes, accompanies, and sustains response, remains resistible, and election is commonly related to foreknown faith. His own account of final apostasy was cautious, while later Remonstrants developed it further. See Arminius's “Grace and Free Will” and the 1610 Remonstrance .
docs.title: Why the Arminian Solution Is Weaker

docs.text: If two equally fallen sinners receive genuinely sufficient enabling grace, and one believes while the other resists, what finally explains the difference? The Arminian reply is that neither response is ungraced, faith merits nothing, and a personal response need not compete with grace. The Reformed concern remains causal rather than meritorious: if grace supplies equal sufficient ability while the undetermined assent differentiates the outcomes, grace is necessary but not finally decisive at the point of difference.
docs.title: Weakness 1: the decisive-difference problem

docs.text: Conditional election protects the priority of Christ and excludes merit. Yet when foreseen faith is election's condition, election recognizes the successful response rather than explaining why saving grace produces it.
docs.title: Weakness 2: election can appear reactive

docs.text: Universal prevenient or enabling grace is systematically coherent, but the Reformed reading disputes that Scripture clearly teaches a universal restoration of libertarian saving ability. The doctrine often functions as the bridge between universal invitation, total inability, and resistible faith; each of those concerns is textually motivated, but the bridge itself requires cumulative inference.
docs.title: Weakness 3: universal enabling grace bears a large exegetical burden

docs.text: Where final apostasy is possible, final salvation depends in part on continued non-resistance. Arminianism remains grace-centered, but from the Reformed standpoint it does not make grace decisive at the final explanatory point.
docs.title: Weakness 4: perseverance becomes contingent

docs.text: Wesleyanism strongly affirms total inability apart from grace, universal prevenient grace, resistible response, assurance, sanctification, and commonly conditional security. The United Methodist doctrinal standards and Wesley's sermons should control its representation.
docs.title: Why the Wesleyan Solution Is Weaker

docs.text: Universal prevenient grace must both answer inability and restore response without determining it. The Reformed question is whether this universal restoration is directly taught or is principally a systematic inference joining universal invitation to libertarian response.
docs.title: Weakness 1: prevenient grace carries major explanatory weight

docs.text: If grace restores genuine saving ability to all, the differing response finally distinguishes belief from unbelief. Wesleyans answer that every good impulse remains graced and faith is not meritorious; the Reformed critique is again about explanatory efficacy, not earning.
docs.title: Weakness 2: the decisive-difference problem remains

docs.text: Wesleyan assurance is real and Spirit-given. Nevertheless, if a regenerate person may finally fall, present assurance does not include the same ground of certain divine preservation affirmed at Dort.
docs.title: Weakness 3: apostasy complicates perseverance and assurance

docs.text: Wesleyanism preserves the priority of grace, universal gospel invitation, meaningful response, and sustained attention to holy love. The Reformed account judges effectual grace stronger because the same grace that initiates renewal also explains faith and final perseverance.
docs.title: Strength acknowledged

docs.text: Roman Catholicism is not one metaphysical theory. It rejects Pelagianism, affirms divine initiative and necessary grace, and contains sophisticated accounts of divine causation. Thomist/Bañezian approaches, Molinism, and the broader Catholic doctrine of grace must be distinguished.
docs.title: Why Catholic Accounts Are Weaker from a Reformed Perspective

docs.text: The Catechism on grace and justification and Trent, Session VI describe initial justification as gratuitous while including interior renewal, free grace-enabled cooperation, sacramental life, and the possibility of grace-enabled merit. The Reformed confessions distinguish justification from sanctification and ground acceptance in Christ's imputed righteousness received through faith alone. The central weakness, under Reformed criteria, is not an absence of grace but a soteriology that does not preserve sola gratia and justification in the same confessional sense.
docs.title: Weakness 1: the confessional disagreement over justification

docs.text: Molinism combines libertarian freedom and meticulous providence through God's pre-decretal knowledge of true counterfactuals of creaturely freedom. Its explanatory cost is the grounding question: what makes those counterfactuals true independently of God's decree and the creature's actual decision? The SEP providence survey presents the proposal and major objections.
docs.title: Weakness 2: Molinism depends on controversial middle knowledge

docs.text: Thomist/Bañezian motion is metaphysically closer to strong divine causation than popular “Catholic free will” summaries suggest. The deeper Reformed disagreements concern justification, merit, sacramental theology, perseverance, and ecclesiology. Thomism is therefore neither Molinism nor Reformed theology. Reformed conclusion: Catholic theology has formidable metaphysical resources, but it does not preserve the same confessional account of sola gratia and justification.
docs.title: Weakness 3: Thomism nears strong divine causality but differs in soteriology

docs.text: Eastern Orthodoxy treats grace as indispensable divine life and action, freedom as healed, salvation as participation and theosis, and synergy as real grace-sustained cooperation—not a 50/50 transaction. John of Damascus and the Orthodox Church in America provide representative sources, though Orthodoxy has no single modern analytic theory.
docs.title: Why the Orthodox Synergistic Account Is Weaker

docs.text: The relational and participatory model explains what salvation is, but if grace may finally be resisted, the same question recurs: what ultimately differentiates cooperation from resistance? Saying that the person truly participates protects agency but does not yet identify why grace reaches its saving effect in one case.
docs.title: Weakness 1: synergy leaves the decisive-response question open

docs.text: Orthodox sources commonly emphasize inherited mortality and corruption rather than inherited guilt and Reformed moral inability. This is neither Pelagianism nor denial of grace. From the Reformed framework, however, it understates the depth of inability expressed in John 6, Romans 8, and Ephesians 2 and therefore reduces the need for effectual renewal.
docs.title: Weakness 2: anthropology of the Fall differs

docs.text: Orthodox readings commonly integrate election with foreknowledge, Christ, and the divine desire to save without giving unconditional individual election the Reformed causal role. Reformed readers judge Romans 8–9, Ephesians 1, and Acts 13:48 more naturally explained by particular election and effectual calling.
docs.title: Weakness 3: election texts carry less causal weight

docs.text: The absence of a Reformed ordo salutis is not by itself an intellectual defect; Orthodoxy organizes salvation around participation, sacrament, and theosis. The narrower assessment is that, under the stated Reformed criteria, the Orthodox model gives less explanatory force to unconditional election and effectual calling.
docs.title: Weakness 4: categories are weighted differently

docs.text: Confessional Lutheranism strongly affirms bondage of the fallen will, monergistic conversion through Word and sacrament, universal grace, and rejection of Pelagian cooperation. The Formula of Concord II says conversion is wholly the Spirit's work, while Lutheran doctrine also affirms resistance and possible apostasy.
docs.title: Why Lutheranism Comes Close but Remains Weaker

docs.text: If conversion is wholly God's work, why does the same grace result in conversion in one case and final resistance in another? Lutheran theology often refuses to infer beyond what it judges Scripture has revealed and locates blame wholly in the resistor; appeal to mystery is not irrationality. Reformed theology nevertheless considers unconditional election and effectual calling a more systematic resolution because divine grace explains the positive difference.
docs.title: Tension 1: resistible grace plus monergistic conversion

docs.text: Possible loss of regeneration means the grace that monergistically creates faith does not ensure completion. Within the Reformed framework, preservation is more consistent with effectual renewal, while warnings remain divinely appointed means.
docs.title: Tension 2: apostasy

docs.text: Formula of Concord XI teaches election to salvation in Christ and refuses a symmetrical decree, tracing condemnation to sin and resistance. Reformed confessions agree on asymmetrical culpability but integrate non-election within a more comprehensive decree. The Reformed gain is systematic integration; its added burden is the author-of-sin objection. Reformed conclusion: Lutheranism is among the closest alternatives, but it is less systematic where monergistic grace, resistibility, election, and apostasy intersect.
docs.title: Tension 3: election and non-election

docs.text: Reformed theology is not “secular hard determinism plus God.” It affirms personal agency, rational deliberation, voluntariness, moral responsibility, purposeful providence, and layered primary and secondary causation. Hard determinism and strong responsibility skepticism gain causal simplicity at the cost of a sufficiently rich account of responsible personal agency. Skeptical models can preserve forward-looking protection and formation, but revision of basic-desert responsibility is precisely what Reformed moral theology rejects. See the SEP overview of responsibility skepticism .
docs.title: Why Hard Determinism and Free-Will Skepticism Are Weaker

docs.text: Open theism protects providential responsiveness by holding that some future free acts are not yet definite truths. From the Reformed perspective, this adds greater costs than classical Arminianism: exhaustive definite foreknowledge, the specificity of prophecy, and confidence in comprehensive providence all require revision. Open theists affirm omniscience as knowledge of reality exactly as it is, so “God guesses” is a caricature; the disagreement concerns whether future free actions are definite objects of knowledge. See the SEP foreknowledge survey .
docs.title: A Brief Reformed Assessment of Open Theism

docs.title: Comparative Explanatory Costs

docs.text: Grace is decisive rather than merely enabling. God's regenerating grace, not an autonomous difference in response, explains saving faith. Providence is comprehensive. One concurrence framework covers ordinary causes, sinful acts, the crucifixion, conversion, and perseverance. Human willing remains real. Determination is not coercion; people deliberate and act from their own reasons and loves. Fallen inability is treated consistently. Regeneration does more than return a sinner to metaphysical neutrality; it renews the disposition. Election is integrated with grace. Election explains why grace reaches saving effect rather than recognizing a future response. Perseverance is grounded in divine preservation. The God who begins renewal completes it through appointed means. Libertarian metaphysics is unnecessary. Voluntariness, actual-sequence sourcehood, and reasons-responsiveness do the required agency work with fewer metaphysical commitments. Scripture contains strong examples of concurrent agency. Joseph and his brothers, Assyria, and the crucifixion join divine purpose to responsible creaturely intention without moral equivalence. From a confessional Reformed standpoint, the principal advantage is not one isolated doctrine, but the way providence, sin, grace, election, voluntary agency, and perseverance mutually reinforce one another.
docs.title: Why the Reformed Model Is Stronger
The Hardest Questions for the Reformed Position

docs.text: If every event falls within providence, why is God not the author of sin? Reformed confessions distinguish God's holy ordination and concurrence from the creature's defective intention, deny that divine causation is morally symmetrical with creaturely causation, and invoke secondary causes. That is a coherent distinction, but the problem of evil demands more than repeating it: the account must show that God has morally sufficient purposes and does not inject evil motives into agents.
docs.title: God and the ordination of evil

docs.text: If a person's character and desires are ultimately within a determined order, is the person a sufficient source for basic desert? Compatibilist replies appeal to ownership, rational agency, and action flowing from the person's own evaluative standpoint. Manipulation arguments press whether that source is deep enough. This is probably the strongest philosophical objection to the model.
docs.title: Ultimate sourcehood

docs.text: First Timothy 2 and 2 Peter 3 appear to express a broad divine desire to save. Reformed distinctions among decree, precept, benevolence, and all kinds of people must be contextually demonstrated rather than used as escape clauses. The universal readings remain important evidence against particular election.
docs.title: Universal-saving-will passages

docs.text: Does transforming desire preserve meaningful relational freedom, or would love require the live possibility of final refusal? The Reformed reply is that healed love can be most free when it is most fully inclined to the good; God's work establishes willing communion rather than bypassing it. A libertarian will dispute whether transformed willingness is enough. These objections are serious, but need not be fatal if concurrent agency is coherent, voluntariness grounds responsibility, and the scriptural case for effectual grace and election is cumulative. The comparative claim is that rival systems face greater or less manageable costs—not that Reformed theology has no mysteries.
docs.title: Love and effectual grace

docs.text: The competing traditions preserve genuine biblical and theological concerns, especially the seriousness of human response, the universality of gospel proclamation, and relational language about grace. From a confessional Reformed perspective, however, they generally preserve these concerns at a greater explanatory cost: grace becomes enabling rather than finally decisive, providence becomes less comprehensive, election becomes conditioned or less causally central, or perseverance becomes contingent on continued human response. The Reformed account is therefore judged strongest because it makes grace finally decisive, preserves comprehensive providence and voluntary responsibility, takes fallen inability seriously, grounds election in God's purpose, treats regeneration as productive of faith, grounds perseverance in divine preservation, avoids requiring libertarian indeterminacy, and offers a unified account of divine and human agency. That conclusion remains conditional on sustaining its compatibilist account of responsibility and its distinction between divine ordination and divine moral approval of evil. This is intentionally a Reformed conclusion.
docs.title: Conclusion

docs.text: Church Fathers on Freedom and Grace Historical caution Libertarianism and compatibilism are modern philosophical categories. Applying them to ancient writers is heuristic rather than a claim that the Fathers subscribed to modern analytic theories. The Fathers addressed fate, voluntary action, moral formation, divine aid, sin, providence, and Christology in different controversies. They did not speak with one voice, and a statement about moral responsibility does not by itself settle a later dispute about the beginning of saving faith. docs.text: Augustine on Free Will and Grace Augustine of Hippo (354–430) is a turning point because he develops both an influential defense of voluntary responsibility and an increasingly strong doctrine of original sin, efficacious grace, predestination, and the gift of perseverance. Disputed classification Later Augustine contains important ideas analogous to later compatibilist accounts, especially willing action shaped by transformed desire. Calling him simply “a compatibilist,” however, projects a modern debate onto changing ancient arguments. Anti-Manichaean context Manichaeism explained evil through opposed cosmic principles and treated the self in ways Augustine came to regard as evasive of responsibility. After leaving the movement, he argues that evil is not a substance created by God: moral evil is a defect of will. Divine foreknowledge does not compel the act God knows; God knows voluntary acts as voluntary. Early Augustine In On Free Choice of the Will ( De libero arbitrio , begun in the 380s and completed in the 390s), Augustine connects law, praise, blame, and just punishment with free choice. The will's misuse, not the good Creator, explains sin. Books II and III broaden the account to providence, foreknowledge, order, and the will's fall. “Early” should not mean “graceless.” Augustine already treats truth and beatitude as divine gifts. The later shift concerns the depth of inherited disorder and the kind of grace needed to begin and persevere in saving willing. From Confessions to To Simplicianus Confessions VIII depicts a divided will: the person wills and does not will, weakened by habit. The problem is neither an external substance nor simple physical constraint. Around 396, Augustine's rereading of Romans in To Simplicianus moves election and the effective call to the center. Faith cannot function as an antecedent merit that explains election. The Pelagian controversy The controversy sharpened several claims: Adam's sin damages descendants rather than serving only as a bad example. Infant baptism bears on inherited sin and the universality of grace. Law and instruction reveal but do not by themselves heal the will. The grace of Christ is interior and effective, not merely creation, forgiveness, or external teaching. Even the beginning of faith cannot be credited to unaided human initiative. Pelagius, Caelestius, and Julian of Aeclanum should not be treated as one undifferentiated position. Augustine's own formulations also develop across the controversy. Later Augustine Bondage and real willing Fallen people retain will and act voluntarily; they do not become non-rational objects. Their problem is a disordered love and inability to achieve saving righteousness without grace. Grace does not merely add an option to an otherwise neutral will: it heals, delights, and produces a good will. Efficacious grace In On Grace and Free Will , Augustine refuses both denial of choice and denial of grace. Commands address a will, while the good willing by which commands are fulfilled is itself God's gift. On Rebuke and Grace describes grace as giving both the ability and the persevering will, yet still treats rebuke and exhortation as means God uses. Predestination and perseverance In On the Predestination of the Saints , the beginning of faith belongs to God's gift and election is not based on foreseen merit. On the Gift of Perseverance distinguishes temporary faith from the further divine gift of persevering to the end. Augustine admits that the distribution of this gift is inscrutable. Transformed desire The later view is not best summarized as coercion. The will comes willingly because grace changes what it loves and supplies delight in the good. This feature later supports compatibilist-like readings. Yet Augustine also speaks of self-determination, divine assistance, and freedom as liberation for righteousness, so modern classifications remain contested. Is Augustine a compatibilist? A careful answer separates comparisons: Question Augustine's mature emphasis Modern comparison Does foreknowledge compel choice? No; God foreknows willing as willing Compatible with several free-will theories Does fallen desire constrain saving action? Yes; the will needs liberation by grace Moral-inability theme Does efficacious grace eliminate willing? No; it produces a good and willing response Compatibilist-like transformed-desire account Are alternative possibilities central to saving conversion? Less central than grace, love, and liberation Unlike many libertarian accounts Is Augustine using causal determinism as modern philosophy defines it? Not as his organizing framework Direct classification is anachronistic The SEP Augustine entry documents both the development and interpretive controversy. Augustine's legacy Medieval Latin theology: grace, merit, predestination, and freedom are debated through Augustinian texts. Aquinas: integrates Augustine with Aristotelian action theory and divine/secondary causation. Luther: appeals to Augustine while radicalizing the polemic against free choice in saving matters. Calvin and Reformed theology: receive Augustine on election, grace, and perseverance through new confessional systems. Catholic grace controversies: Thomist/Bañezian, Molinist, and later Jansenist disputes all claim or contest Augustinian inheritances. Modern philosophy: Augustine is studied as a major theorist of will, action, evil, and divided agency. Influence is not identity: Augustine is not “Calvin before Calvin,” and neither Aquinas nor Luther simply repeats him. docs.text: Early Fathers The second- and third-century authors here commonly defend responsibility against pagan fate, Gnostic divisions of humanity, or deterministic readings of providence. That makes their work important to free-will history, but it does not turn them into later Arminians or modern libertarians. Justin Martyr Dates: c. 100–165 Region/tradition: Greek-speaking Christian apologist in Rome Relevant works: First Apology , Second Apology , Dialogue with Trypho Human freedom and responsibility Justin argues that praise and punishment would be unjust if acts followed fate rather than choice. His apologetic therefore gives strong weight to alternatives and voluntary responsibility. Grace and providence Human rational capacity is created, and truth is disclosed through the divine Logos. Justin's anti-fatalism should not be mistaken for autonomous self-salvation. Modern comparison “Libertarian-leaning” and “strongly anti-fatalist” are useful comparisons. Justin does not supply a contemporary theory of agent causation or address later disputes about prevenient grace. Primary sources First Apology , especially chapters 10, 28, and 43 ; Second Apology . Irenaeus of Lyons Dates: c. 130–c. 202 Region/tradition: Asia Minor and Gaul; bishop of Lyons Relevant works: Against Heresies , Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching Human freedom Against Gnostic schemes that divide people into fixed spiritual types, Irenaeus stresses growth, obedience, and the capacity to accept or refuse. Against Heresies IV.37 explicitly connects choice with exhortation and just judgment. Grace, sin, and formation Freedom exists within an economy of creation, incarnation, recapitulation, and maturation. Humanity is dependent and immature; Christ restores and brings the creature toward communion. It is misleading to isolate choice from that economy. Modern comparison Irenaeus has libertarian-leaning themes because he rejects coercive necessity and stresses alternatives. His developmental anthropology is not a theory of neutral, unaided spiritual ability. Primary sources Against Heresies IV.37 and IV.39; Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching . Tertullian Dates: c. 155–after 220 Region/tradition: Latin North Africa Relevant works: Against Marcion , On the Soul , On Exhortation to Chastity Human freedom and moral responsibility Tertullian links divine law, judgment, and culpability to voluntary action. In controversy with Marcion he argues that a rational creature given law must possess the capacity of choice; misuse belongs to the creature, not to a defect in the Creator. Grace and caution His emphasis is anti-Marcionite responsibility, not the later Augustinian question of the first movement of saving faith. “Libertarian-leaning” captures the anti-necessitarian strand but not a complete soteriology. Primary sources Against Marcion , Book II ; On the Soul . Clement of Alexandria Dates: c. 150–c. 215 Region/tradition: Alexandria Relevant works: Protrepticus , Paedagogus , Stromata Choice, formation, and grace Clement presents Christian life as divinely taught moral and intellectual formation. Exhortation assumes responsive choice, while the Logos instructs, heals, and supplies the path and power of maturity. Providence and cooperation are not competitors. Modern comparison A synergistic trajectory is clearer than a precise modern metaphysical label. Clement's language of choice coexists with demanding accounts of divine pedagogy and ecclesial formation. Primary sources Stromata , Book I and Book VII; The Instructor . Origen Dates: c. 185–c. 253 Region/tradition: Alexandria and Caesarea Relevant works: On First Principles , Against Celsus , Commentary on Romans Human freedom Origen makes rational creaturely self-determination central to moral diversity and judgment. On First Principles III rejects astral or constitutional necessity and argues that commands presuppose responsibility. Grace, sin, and providence God educates, judges, heals, and assists rational creatures through providence and the Logos. Origen's strong freedom language does not eliminate grace. His preexistence, fall, and restoration speculations also complicate direct comparison with later Western accounts of original sin. Modern comparison and caution He is strongly anti-fatalist and incompatibilist- or libertarian-leaning. The exact scope of alternatives, providence, and final restoration is textually and historically disputed, especially because later condemnations and the transmission of On First Principles complicate interpretation. Primary sources On First Principles III.1 ; Against Celsus . Next Continue with the Greek Fathers , compare the Latin Fathers , or see how Augustine reconfigures the Western debate.

docs.text: Greek Fathers Greek patristic accounts often connect freedom to creation in God's image, moral and ascetic formation, healing, and participation in divine life. This is a trajectory, not a unanimous school. Historical caution: “Synergistic” can describe a pattern of divine initiative and human cooperation. It must not be read as the claim that grace and nature are two independent, equal causes. Athanasius of Alexandria Dates: c. 296–373 Relevant works: On the Incarnation , Against the Heathen , Life of Antony Athanasius depicts rational creatures as made for contemplation and communion yet turned toward corruption by misuse. The incarnation restores the image, defeats death, and makes knowledge and holiness possible. His account foregrounds ontological healing more than the later question of whether an isolated decision has alternative possibilities. Modern comparison: freedom-as-restoration within divine action; anti-necessitarian themes, but no simple analytic label. Primary sources: On the Incarnation ; Against the Heathen . Basil the Great Dates: c. 330–379 Relevant works: Hexaemeron , On the Holy Spirit , Longer Rules , homilies Basil's preaching and ascetic rules presuppose deliberate response, habit, repentance, and accountable action. The Holy Spirit perfects and sanctifies; moral agency is exercised within worship and communal discipline rather than as metaphysical independence. Modern comparison: synergistic trajectory with strong ascetic and pneumatological context. Primary sources: On the Holy Spirit ; selected homilies . Gregory of Nazianzus Dates: 329–390 Relevant works: Theological Orations , moral and festal orations Gregory holds together divine initiative and a willing human response. His Christology makes the healing of the complete human person central: what is not assumed is not healed. Exhortation and repentance are genuine, yet salvation is gift and transformation. Modern comparison: synergistic and anti-coercive themes; not a worked-out libertarian theory. Primary sources: Orations , especially Orations 29–31 and 45. Gregory of Nyssa Dates: c. 335–c. 395 Relevant works: On the Making of Man , Great Catechism , Life of Moses Human freedom and responsibility Gregory links being made in God's image to rational self-direction and treats evil as a privation arising through mutable choice rather than a divinely created substance. Moral progress and purification presuppose responsive agency. Grace and spiritual ability Creation, incarnation, sacrament, and divine attraction frame human movement. Gregory's freedom is teleological: authentic freedom matures toward the Good, not mere indifference among options. Modern comparison and caution “Libertarian-leaning” is reasonable for his rejection of compulsion and strong self-determination. Debates over universal restoration, infinity, and the stability of the will prevent a simple placement. Primary sources On the Making of Man ; Great Catechism ; Life of Moses . John Chrysostom Dates: c. 347–407 Relevant works: Homilies on Romans , Homilies on John , Homilies on Ephesians Chrysostom's homiletic method assumes that warnings, commands, repentance, and perseverance address responsible hearers. He repeatedly refuses fatalistic readings of providence and emphasizes willing response. At the same time, he attributes the call, aid, forgiveness, and transformation to God. Modern comparison: strongly synergistic and anti-fatalist; a modern theory of indeterministic causation should not be inferred from sermon rhetoric alone. Primary sources: Homilies on Romans ; Homilies on John . Cyril of Alexandria Dates: c. 376–444 Relevant works: Commentary on John , Against Nestorius , letters Cyril's decisive context is Christological and sacramental. Union with Christ and the Spirit restores and vivifies humanity. He affirms accountable response, but his treatment should not be reconstructed from isolated vocabulary into a modern free-will model. Modern comparison: grace-centered participatory agency; classification beyond that is disputed. Primary sources: letters and conciliar texts ; Commentary on John . Maximus the Confessor Dates: c. 580–662 Region/tradition: Byzantine monk and theologian Relevant works: Ambigua , Questions to Thalassius , Disputation with Pyrrhus , Opuscula Natural and gnomic willing For Maximus, natural will is the rational appetite or capacity for the good belonging to human nature. Gnomic willing names a mode of deliberative, hesitant self-determination associated with a person who does not clearly know or stably possess the good. It is not simply a second faculty alongside natural will. Christology Maximus defended Christ's complete human natural will against Monothelitism. Christ wills humanly and divinely without sinful opposition; attributing gnomic deliberation to Christ would, in Maximus's mature account, introduce ignorance or uncertainty inappropriate to the incarnate Logos. The Sixth Ecumenical Council later confessed two natural wills and operations in Christ. Grace, freedom, and deification Human fulfillment is not escape from natural willing but its healing and free conformity to God. Ascetic practice, sacrament, virtue, and grace reorder the person's mode of willing toward the logos of nature. Cooperation belongs within deification: the creature acts because divine life heals and empowers creaturely agency. Modern comparison Maximus cannot be flattened into libertarianism versus compatibilism. His account joins nature, hypostasis, deliberation, Christology, and eschatological freedom in categories unlike the modern causal-determinist debate. Primary sources and scholarship Disputation with Pyrrhus ; Opuscula 3 and 7; Ambigua 7 and 42; Questions to Thalassius 21. For orientation, see Maximus's place in the historical development and the Eastern Orthodox profile . Modern interpretation of gnōmē and its development across Maximus's career remains disputed. John of Damascus Dates: c. 675–749 Relevant works: Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith John distinguishes foreknowledge from predetermination: God foreknows what is “in our power” without predetermining it in the same way as events of providence. Deliberation, choice, and action ground responsibility; providence includes willing, permission, and wise governance. Modern comparison: synergistic and libertarian-leaning themes, but expressed within patristic psychology and providence rather than analytic incompatibilism. docs.text: Dates: c. 296–373 Relevant works: On the Incarnation , Against the Heathen , Life of Antony Athanasius depicts rational creatures as made for contemplation and communion yet turned toward corruption by misuse. The incarnation restores the image, defeats death, and makes knowledge and holiness possible. His account foregrounds ontological healing more than the later question of whether an isolated decision has alternative possibilities. Modern comparison: freedom-as-restoration within divine action; anti-necessitarian themes, but no simple analytic label. Primary sources: On the Incarnation ; Against the Heathen .
docs.title: Athanasius of Alexandria

docs.text: Dates: c. 330–379 Relevant works: Hexaemeron , On the Holy Spirit , Longer Rules , homilies Basil's preaching and ascetic rules presuppose deliberate response, habit, repentance, and accountable action. The Holy Spirit perfects and sanctifies; moral agency is exercised within worship and communal discipline rather than as metaphysical independence. Modern comparison: synergistic trajectory with strong ascetic and pneumatological context. Primary sources: On the Holy Spirit ; selected homilies .
docs.title: Basil the Great

docs.text: Dates: 329–390 Relevant works: Theological Orations , moral and festal orations Gregory holds together divine initiative and a willing human response. His Christology makes the healing of the complete human person central: what is not assumed is not healed. Exhortation and repentance are genuine, yet salvation is gift and transformation. Modern comparison: synergistic and anti-coercive themes; not a worked-out libertarian theory. Primary sources: Orations , especially Orations 29–31 and 45.

docs.text: Dates: c. 335–c. 395 Relevant works: On the Making of Man , Great Catechism , Life of Moses
docs.title: Gregory of Nyssa

docs.text: Gregory links being made in God's image to rational self-direction and treats evil as a privation arising through mutable choice rather than a divinely created substance. Moral progress and purification presuppose responsive agency.
docs.title: Human freedom and responsibility

docs.text: Creation, incarnation, sacrament, and divine attraction frame human movement. Gregory's freedom is teleological: authentic freedom matures toward the Good, not mere indifference among options.
docs.title: Grace and spiritual ability

docs.text: “Libertarian-leaning” is reasonable for his rejection of compulsion and strong self-determination. Debates over universal restoration, infinity, and the stability of the will prevent a simple placement.
