docs.text: Dates: c. 347–407 Relevant works: Homilies on Romans , Homilies on John , Homilies on Ephesians Chrysostom's homiletic method assumes that warnings, commands, repentance, and perseverance address responsible hearers. He repeatedly refuses fatalistic readings of providence and emphasizes willing response. At the same time, he attributes the call, aid, forgiveness, and transformation to God. Modern comparison: strongly synergistic and anti-fatalist; a modern theory of indeterministic causation should not be inferred from sermon rhetoric alone. Primary sources: Homilies on Romans ; Homilies on John .
docs.title: John Chrysostom

docs.text: Dates: c. 376–444 Relevant works: Commentary on John , Against Nestorius , letters Cyril's decisive context is Christological and sacramental. Union with Christ and the Spirit restores and vivifies humanity. He affirms accountable response, but his treatment should not be reconstructed from isolated vocabulary into a modern free-will model. Modern comparison: grace-centered participatory agency; classification beyond that is disputed. Primary sources: letters and conciliar texts ; Commentary on John .
docs.title: Cyril of Alexandria

docs.text: Dates: c. 580–662 Region/tradition: Byzantine monk and theologian Relevant works: Ambigua , Questions to Thalassius , Disputation with Pyrrhus , Opuscula
docs.title: Maximus the Confessor

docs.text: For Maximus, natural will is the rational appetite or capacity for the good belonging to human nature. Gnomic willing names a mode of deliberative, hesitant self-determination associated with a person who does not clearly know or stably possess the good. It is not simply a second faculty alongside natural will.
docs.title: Natural and gnomic willing

docs.text: Maximus defended Christ's complete human natural will against Monothelitism. Christ wills humanly and divinely without sinful opposition; attributing gnomic deliberation to Christ would, in Maximus's mature account, introduce ignorance or uncertainty inappropriate to the incarnate Logos. The Sixth Ecumenical Council later confessed two natural wills and operations in Christ.
docs.title: Christology

docs.text: Human fulfillment is not escape from natural willing but its healing and free conformity to God. Ascetic practice, sacrament, virtue, and grace reorder the person's mode of willing toward the logos of nature. Cooperation belongs within deification: the creature acts because divine life heals and empowers creaturely agency.
docs.title: Grace, freedom, and deification

docs.text: Maximus cannot be flattened into libertarianism versus compatibilism. His account joins nature, hypostasis, deliberation, Christology, and eschatological freedom in categories unlike the modern causal-determinist debate.
docs.title: Modern comparison

docs.text: Disputation with Pyrrhus ; Opuscula 3 and 7; Ambigua 7 and 42; Questions to Thalassius 21. For orientation, see Maximus's place in the historical development and the Eastern Orthodox profile . Modern interpretation of gnōmē and its development across Maximus's career remains disputed.

docs.text: Dates: c. 675–749 Relevant works: Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith John distinguishes foreknowledge from predetermination: God foreknows what is “in our power” without predetermining it in the same way as events of providence. Deliberation, choice, and action ground responsibility; providence includes willing, permission, and wise governance. Modern comparison: synergistic and libertarian-leaning themes, but expressed within patristic psychology and providence rather than analytic incompatibilism. Primary source: Exact Exposition II.22–30 .

docs.text: Latin Fathers Latin Christianity developed a particularly influential vocabulary of will, culpability, original sin, grace, and predestination. Tertullian, Augustine, and Cassian illustrate development and disagreement rather than a single “Latin view.” Tertullian Tertullian's anti-Marcionite arguments connect law and judgment with voluntary creaturely action. See the fuller early-fathers profile . His work is an antecedent to Latin reflection on voluntas , not a statement of later Augustinian soteriology. Augustine of Hippo Dates: 354–430 Region: Roman North Africa Relevant works: On Free Choice of the Will , Confessions , On the Spirit and the Letter , On Grace and Free Will , On the Predestination of the Saints Augustine's early anti-Manichaean work defends creaturely free choice as the source of evil. During and after the Pelagian controversy he increasingly argues that the fallen will cannot heal itself, the beginning of faith is a gift, and perseverance depends on efficacious grace. He continues to affirm willing and responsibility; the question becomes how grace liberates the will. Because this development anchors later Western debates, see the dedicated Augustine page . John Cassian Dates: c. 360–c. 435 Region/tradition: probably Scythia; Egyptian monastic formation; founded monasteries near Marseille Relevant works: Institutes , Conferences , especially Conference 13 Human freedom and grace Cassian resists both self-sufficient will and an account he thinks makes exhortation idle. Conference 13 assembles biblical cases in which divine initiative is conspicuous and cases in which a human movement seems to be met by grace. Throughout, attainment and perseverance remain gifts of God. Sin and spiritual ability His ascetic setting concerns trained, baptized monks as well as conversion. Habit, temptation, prayer, and discipline matter. It is therefore hazardous to turn every claim about ascetic cooperation into a claim about the unaided beginning of faith. Modern comparison and scholarly caution Cassian is a major witness to a synergistic Latin trajectory. The label “Semi-Pelagian” was coined later and can obscure his strong doctrines of grace; interpreters disagree over whether Conference 13 assigns any first saving movement to unaided will. State the narrower claim being evaluated rather than using the label as a verdict. Primary sources Conference 13 ; Conferences 1–10 ; Institutes . Cassian was not simply a reaction to a finished “Augustinian system,” and Orange did not settle every later Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed, or Arminian question. docs.text: Ten Theologians Who Shaped Christian Thought This is a curated study list, not an objective “best theologians” ranking. Selection weighs long-term doctrinal impact, influence across traditions, role in major controversies, continuing study, and relevance to creation, Christology, anthropology, grace, salvation, or freedom. The chronological order avoids pretending to measure greatness. 1. Irenaeus of Lyons Dates/tradition: c.130–c.202; early catholic bishop. Contribution: anti-Gnostic rule of faith, recapitulation, creation and redemption as one economy. Works: Against Heresies ; Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching . Influence: canon, apostolic tradition, Christology, and theological anthropology across East and West. Free will/grace: strong responsible choice within divine formation. See Early Fathers . 2. Athanasius of Alexandria Dates/tradition: c.296–373; Greek patristic. Contribution: defense of Nicene faith and incarnational restoration. Works: On the Incarnation ; Orations Against the Arians . Influence: Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy; salvation as participation and victory over corruption. Free will/grace: created agency healed in the incarnate Word. 3. Gregory of Nazianzus Dates/tradition: 329–390; Cappadocian Father. Contribution: decisive Trinitarian language and complete humanity of Christ. Works: Theological Orations ; letters and poetry. Influence: councils, Eastern and Western Trinitarian theology. Free will/grace: human response and complete healing within divine initiative. 4. Augustine of Hippo Dates/tradition: 354–430; Latin patristic. Contribution: will, evil, Trinity, original sin, grace, predestination, church, and history. Works: Confessions ; City of God ; On the Trinity ; anti-Pelagian works. Influence: medieval West, Catholicism, Reformation, and modern philosophy. Free will/grace: major Western turning point. See Augustine . 5. Maximus the Confessor Dates/tradition: c.580–662; Byzantine patristic. Contribution: two wills of Christ, cosmic Christology, deification, natural and gnomic willing. Works: Ambigua ; Questions to Thalassius ; Disputation with Pyrrhus . Influence: Byzantine theology and modern retrieval. Free will/grace: sophisticated account that resists a simple modern binary. See Greek Fathers . 6. Thomas Aquinas Dates/tradition: c.1225–1274; Latin Catholic/Scholastic. Contribution: systematic synthesis of creation, causation, virtue, grace, sacraments, and beatitude. Works: Summa theologiae ; Summa contra Gentiles . Influence: Catholic doctrine, philosophy, and ecumenical study. Free will/grace: primary and secondary causation; disputed modern classification. See Aquinas . 7. Martin Luther Dates/tradition: 1483–1546; Lutheran reformer. Contribution: justification by faith, theology of the cross, authority of Scripture, reform of church and worship. Works: Bondage of the Will ; Freedom of a Christian ; catechisms. Influence: Protestant Reformation and global Lutheranism. Free will/grace: saving inability and monergistic conversion. See Luther . 8. John Calvin Dates/tradition: 1509–1564; Reformed. Contribution: providence, union with Christ, church, sacraments, election, and scriptural exposition. Works: Institutes ; biblical commentaries. Influence: Continental Reformed, Presbyterian, Puritan, and Baptist traditions. Free will/grace: voluntary bondage and effectual renewal. See Calvin . 9. John Wesley Dates/tradition: 1703–1791; Anglican/Methodist. Contribution: evangelical revival, disciplined societies, assurance, sanctification, and Christian perfection. Works: Standard Sermons ; journals; Notes upon the New Testament . Influence: Methodism, Holiness, and many Pentecostal streams. Free will/grace: universal prevenient grace and resistible response. See Wesley . 10. Karl Barth Dates/tradition: 1886–1968; Swiss Reformed. Contribution: twentieth-century dogmatic renewal centered on divine revelation and election in Jesus Christ. Works: Church Dogmatics ; Epistle to the Romans . Influence: Protestant and ecumenical theology far beyond his own tradition. Free will/grace: reframes election Christologically and freedom as correspondence to God's freedom, not chiefly alternative possibility. Serious alternative candidates Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Anselm, Jacobus Arminius, Jonathan Edwards, John Henry Newman, Friedrich Schleiermacher, Søren Kierkegaard, and Dietrich Bonhoeffer could replace members under other defensible criteria. The separate free-will list includes thinkers whose direct relevance outweighs their cross-doctrinal reach.

docs.text: Anabaptist Builders Anabaptism includes Swiss Brethren, South German/Austrian, Hutterite, Mennonite, and other networks. Strong common themes—believer's baptism, discipleship, disciplined church, and nonconformity—do not erase theological differences. Menno Simons Dates: 1496–1561 Role: Dutch former priest and major Mennonite consolidator Works: Foundation of Christian Doctrine ; The New Birth Menno organizes scattered communities after the Münster crisis and centers true faith on new birth, obedience, peace, and a visible holy life. Grace in Christ is indispensable; the human response is voluntary and embodied in discipleship. Calling this “Pelagian” would ignore his dependence on divine mercy and regeneration. Conrad Grebel and Felix Manz Grebel (c. 1498–1526) and Manz (c. 1498–1527) were early Swiss Brethren leaders in the break with Zwingli over baptism and church discipline. Surviving sources focus more on church and obedience than a systematic free-will metaphysics. Balthasar Hubmaier Dates: c. 1480–1528 Hubmaier, a learned South German Anabaptist, addresses grace and freedom more explicitly, including On Free Will . He distinguishes the damage of the Fall and restoration through Christ, while defending responsible response. His acceptance of magisterial coercion in some contexts and other differences make him unrepresentative of all Anabaptism. docs.text: Anglican Builders Anglicanism emerged through crown, Parliament, bishops, liturgy, inherited catholic structures, and continental reform. Thomas Cranmer and Richard Hooker are formative, not solitary founders. Thomas Cranmer Dates: 1489–1556 Role: Archbishop of Canterbury, English reformer, liturgical and confessional architect Works: 1549 and 1552 Books of Common Prayer ; homilies; contribution to the Forty-Two Articles Cranmer's mature theology stresses fallen inability, justification by faith, and divine initiative. The liturgy makes grace ecclesial and sacramental rather than an abstract decision mechanism. Article X's language of preventing and cooperating grace descends through this Reformation setting, though the final Thirty-Nine Articles postdate his death. Richard Hooker Dates: 1554–1600 Role: Anglican priest and formative defender of the Elizabethan settlement Work: Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity Hooker situates voluntary action within divine eternal law, created rational participation, church, sacrament, and grace. Reason is not an autonomous rival to Scripture; nature and grace have ordered relations. His soteriology shares Reformation commitments while his account of law and sacrament helps later Anglicans articulate a distinctively broad synthesis. Later diversity Reformed Anglicans, Laudian High Church thinkers, Arminian streams, evangelical revivalists, Wesleyans, and Anglo-Catholics develop different models of election, efficacy, and perseverance. Neither Cranmer nor Hooker exhausts them. Sources and links Church of England, Articles of Religion Book of Common Prayer Anglican tradition profile

docs.text: Thomas Aquinas Thomas Aquinas is a formative medieval Latin theologian whose account of intellect, will, providence, secondary causation, grace, and predestination anchors Thomist debates. He is neither the founder of Catholicism nor easily classed as a modern libertarian or compatibilist. Historical context Dates: c. 1225–1274 Tradition: Dominican, Latin Catholic, Scholastic Context: Aristotelian reception, university theology, mendicant life Major works Summa theologiae ; Summa contra Gentiles ; Disputed Questions on Truth ; Disputed Questions on Evil ; commentaries on Aristotle and Scripture. Anthropology and free will The intellect presents an apprehended good; the will is a rational appetite ordered toward universal good. Because particular goods do not exhaust that object, the will is not necessitated by any finite good simply as such. Deliberation and practical judgment make a person master of acts and responsible. Aquinas also holds that God is the universal first cause who moves every created cause. Divine causation does not replace a creature's mode of action: necessary causes act necessarily and contingent voluntary causes act contingently and voluntarily. Secondary causation is real because the first cause establishes and sustains it. Grace Grace is needed not only to heal sin but to elevate humanity to the supernatural end of beatitude. In justification God moves the adult will to assent and repent; because God moves a rational creature according to its nature, the movement of free choice belongs within, not outside, the effect of grace. Predestination and election Predestination is part of providence and its cause is divine goodness rather than antecedent human merit. Aquinas nevertheless insists that prayer, merit as enabled by grace, and secondary causes are real means within providence. His account of reprobation distinguishes permission of defect from divine causation of sin. Molinists challenge that explanation while claiming fidelity to Aquinas. Contemporary analytic interpreters likewise divide over whether Aquinas's contingency and divine motion best resemble source compatibilism, libertarianism, or a framework that cuts across both. Common misunderstandings Aquinas does not make creatures inert occasions of divine action. He does not teach that unaided will earns the first grace. His affirmation of predestination does not make sin positively caused by God. “Aquinas was a compatibilist/libertarian” needs an argument and qualification. docs.text: Jacobus Arminius Jacobus Arminius gives grace—not autonomous natural choice—the decisive priority. His dispute concerns the universality and resistibility of grace, conditional election, and providence within the Dutch Reformed context. Historical context Dates: 1560–1609 Tradition: Dutch Reformed theologian; formative antecedent of Remonstrant and evangelical Arminian traditions Context: Leiden controversies over predestination, grace, and confessional interpretation Major works Declaration of Sentiments ; Public Disputations ; Private Disputations ; correspondence and apologetic writings. The Five Articles of the Remonstrance were issued by followers in 1610 after his death and should not be treated as his own text. Anthropology and free will Arminius denies that fallen free choice can begin or perfect any true spiritual good without grace. Mind, affections, and will all require renewal. He calls grace absolutely necessary and says it goes before, accompanies, and follows the good act. His account nevertheless preserves the possibility of resisting grace. A grace-enabled will can assent or refuse; this makes his orientation libertarian-leaning in saving response, though his scholastic account of concurrence is more detailed than a slogan about “choice.” Grace and salvation Christ's grace illuminates, inclines, assists, and sustains. Justification is by faith and excludes meritorious self-reliance. Arminian synergy therefore begins only with grace already active. Arminianism does not mean that fallen humans can save themselves by autonomous natural free will. Predestination and foreknowledge Arminius rejects an unconditional decree that logically places particular election and reprobation before the Fall and the provision of Christ. He presents election in Christ of believers, with foreknowledge of faith and perseverance. Providence remains meticulous, but God does not necessitate culpable acts in a way that destroys their contingency. Perseverance Arminius treats final apostasy cautiously and says the question requires further scriptural inquiry. Later Remonstrants affirm its possibility more clearly. It is therefore inaccurate to assign every later Arminian conclusion to Arminius without qualification. Position across the dimensions Dimension Arminius Alternatives Strong grace-enabled emphasis Fallen ability None for true spiritual good without grace Grace Preceding, accompanying, sustaining Grace resistible Yes Foreknowledge Compatible with contingent acts Election Conditional/Christ-centered Apostasy Cautious/underdeveloped in his own work Modern comparison Libertarian-leaning Influence The Remonstrants formulate five contested articles; the Synod of Dort answers them. Later evangelical Arminianism, Wesley, Methodism, Holiness churches, many General Baptists, and many Pentecostals receive and transform Arminian themes. Common misunderstandings Arminius does not teach Pelagian natural ability. His theology is not identical to every later Remonstrant position. Conditional election does not mean election is merited. Resistibility is a claim about grace-enabled agency, not grace's absence. Reformed Assessment Arminius's strongest contribution is his unambiguous insistence that every saving movement depends on preceding, accompanying, and sustaining grace; Arminianism is not Pelagianism. From a confessional Reformed perspective, resistible universal enablement leaves the decisive difference between belief and resistance in the creaturely response, makes election responsive to foreknown faith, and commonly makes final salvation conditional on continued non-resistance. docs.text: Baptist Builders Baptist origins include distinct General and Particular streams. The figures below are early leaders and major representatives, not founders of a single uniform doctrine. General Baptist stream John Smyth Dates: c. 1570–1612 Smyth moved through Puritan Separatism, believers' baptism, and contact with Dutch Mennonites. His developing theology opposed strict predestinarianism and helped open a General Baptist trajectory. Because his positions changed rapidly, no single late statement should define all later Baptists. Thomas Helwys Dates: c. 1575–c. 1616 Helwys helped establish an English General Baptist congregation and defended religious liberty in A Short Declaration of the Mystery of Iniquity . His soteriology stresses universal provision and responsible response. Liberty of conscience is historically important but is not itself proof of a specific metaphysics of free will. Particular / Reformed Baptist stream Benjamin Keach Dates: 1640–1704 Keach was a major Particular Baptist pastor associated with the 1689 confession. He combines Reformed effectual grace and perseverance with evangelistic proclamation. John Gill Dates: 1697–1771 Gill systematizes high Calvinist Baptist theology. His precise relation to later hyper-Calvinism is debated; he should not stand for every Particular Baptist. Andrew Fuller Dates: 1754–1815 In The Gospel Worthy of All Acceptation , Fuller distinguishes natural and moral inability and defends the duty of every hearer to believe. He receives Edwards while energizing missionary Particular Baptist life. Charles Spurgeon Dates: 1834–1892 Spurgeon combines robust Reformed election and effectual grace with indiscriminate gospel invitation. Popular appeals should be read within, not against, his confessional Calvinism. docs.text: John Calvin and Jonathan Edwards John Calvin supplies a formative Reformed account of providence, voluntary bondage, regeneration, election, and perseverance. Jonathan Edwards later gives one of the tradition's most systematic analyses of will, desire, and necessity. John Calvin Dates: 1509–1564 Tradition: French Reformed reformer in Geneva Major work: Institutes of the Christian Religion Anthropology and free will Calvin says fallen people act voluntarily rather than by external compulsion, yet their will is captive to disordered desire and cannot turn to saving good without the Spirit. Responsibility therefore rests on willing action and the creature's corrupt disposition, not a libertarian power of contrary choice. Providence Providence encompasses events and creaturely causes. Calvin rejects fate as an impersonal chain and insists that God's governance does not erase the different intentions of agents. His biblical and pastoral vocabulary should not simply be replaced with modern causal determinism. Grace, election, and perseverance Regeneration renews mind and will; effectual calling produces willing faith. Election is unconditional and magnifies gratuitous mercy. Calvin treats reprobation within the decree but distinguishes divine righteous purpose from the wicked intentions and culpability of agents. Union with Christ and the Spirit's preservation ground perseverance. Dimensions Dimension Calvin Alternatives Not required for saving responsibility Sourcehood/voluntariness Strong voluntary-action emphasis Fallen ability Unable to turn savingly Grace Effectual renewal Providence Comprehensive divine governance Election Unconditional Apostasy Apparent/temporary faith distinguished from persevering faith Modern comparison Compatibilist-leaning; terminology later Theodore Beza and Francis Turretin Theodore Beza (1519–1605) systematizes Reformed predestination in later controversy; historians debate the degree of continuity with Calvin. Francis Turretin (1623–1687) develops scholastic distinctions among necessity, coercion, contingency, and divine concurrence. Neither should be used as a transparent substitute for Calvin's own formulations. Jonathan Edwards Dates: 1703–1758 Tradition: New England Reformed/Congregational Major work: Freedom of the Will (1754) Desire, necessity, and inability Edwards argues that the will follows the greatest apparent good or strongest motive as apprehended. Natural inability involves lack of capacity or opportunity and excuses; moral inability is inability arising from contrary inclination and does not excuse, because the act still expresses the agent's heart. Edwards rejects a self-determining will conceived as choosing its own prior act of choice, which generates a regress. Liberty is doing as one wills without external hindrance, while moral necessity can coexist with praise and blame. Grace Regeneration supplies a new spiritual disposition; faith follows effectual grace. This is a recognizably theological compatibilism, though contemporary compatibilists may reject Edwards's metaphysics or theology. Dimensions Dimension Edwards Alternatives Not required for responsibility Sourcehood Action expresses prevailing inclination Fallen ability Natural faculties remain; moral inability to spiritual good Grace Effectual change of disposition Election Reformed/unconditional Apostasy Perseverance of true saints Modern comparison Compatibilist Common misunderstandings Calvin's voluntary bondage is not the claim that desire is externally forced. “Natural ability” in Edwards does not mean moral neutrality or saving ability. Later Reformed compatibilism develops Calvin; it should not be attributed to him word-for-word. Connection to the Reformed evaluation Calvin's account of voluntary bondage and providence and Edwards's analysis of moral inability supply important parts of the later Reformed synthesis, but neither thinker is the argument's sole authority. A Reformed Evaluation of Free Will tests their shared model against confessional, biblical, and philosophical criteria and includes its author-of-sin and ultimate-sourcehood difficulties. docs.text: Edwards argues that the will follows the greatest apparent good or strongest motive as apprehended. docs.text: Martin Luther Martin Luther's controversy with Erasmus makes the “bondage of the will” central to Reformation debate. His denial concerns unaided power in relation to God and salvation, not the existence of willing or ordinary deliberation. Historical context Dates: 1483–1546 Tradition: German reformer; formative Lutheran theologian Controversy: Erasmus's On Free Will (1524) and Luther's On the Bondage of the Will (1525) Major works On the Bondage of the Will ; Heidelberg Disputation ; Freedom of a Christian ; Large Catechism ; lectures on Romans, Galatians, and Genesis. Anthropology and free will Luther distinguishes matters “below” from matters “above.” Humans choose, plan, govern households, and act voluntarily in temporal affairs. Before God, however, the fallen person cannot produce faith, merit grace, or turn themselves from unbelief. “Bondage” is a directed will captive to sin, not absence of psychological willing. In arguing against Erasmus's deliberately modest account of free choice, Luther also uses sweeping language about divine foreknowledge and necessity. Interpreters dispute how those arguments relate to his pastoral, Christological, and sacramental theology and to later Lutheran confessions. Grace, conversion, and salvation The Spirit creates faith through the gospel. Justification is God's forensic gift received by faith, not the reward for a self-originating decision. The person so renewed trusts and acts willingly; works follow faith rather than cause justification. Predestination Luther sometimes speaks with strongly Augustinian predestinarian language, but later confessional Lutheranism directs election toward Christ and the means of grace and rejects symmetrical reprobation. Luther should not be relabeled “a Calvinist” on the basis of overlap. docs.text: Luis de Molina and Domingo Báñez The late-sixteenth-century de auxiliis controversy concerned how efficacious grace, providence, predestination, and free choice cohere within Catholic doctrine. Molinists and Thomist/Bañezians are internal Catholic schools, not Catholic versus non-Catholic positions. Luis de Molina Dates: 1535–1600 Tradition: Jesuit, Latin Catholic Major work: Concordia liberi arbitrii cum gratiae donis (1588) Middle knowledge and freedom Molina distinguishes God's natural knowledge of necessities, middle knowledge of counterfactuals of creaturely freedom, and free knowledge of the created world God chooses. Before the creative decree, God knows what each possible free creature would do in specified circumstances. By choosing which feasible world to actualize, God exercises meticulous providence without causally determining the libertarian choice. Molinist freedom requires that, with all prerequisites for action present, the agent retain power for either outcome. The enduring objection asks what grounds counterfactuals about never-actualized free choices and whether their prior truth limits divine or creaturely control. Grace and salvation Molina affirms original sin, the necessity and priority of grace, predestination, and Catholic justification. Middle knowledge is not a Pelagian theory of salvation; it is a proposed account of providence and the distribution of grace with free response. Domingo Báñez Dates: 1528–1604 Tradition: Dominican, Thomist Role: Aquinas commentator and major representative in the grace controversy Báñez emphasizes God's physical premotion and the intrinsic efficacy of grace. God moves secondary causes according to their modes, so the will acts voluntarily rather than by external compulsion. Critics argue the account threatens libertarian alternatives; Bañezians reply that dependence on first causation perfects rather than cancels creaturely agency. Bañezian motion is not described by its defenders as coercion. Catholic teaching did not canonize one school as the only permissible theory. Reformed Assessment Molinism's strongest contribution is a technically sophisticated attempt to join meticulous providence to robust libertarian freedom without identifying foreknowledge with causation. From a confessional Reformed perspective, it carries the grounding burden for pre-decretal counterfactuals of creaturely freedom and makes providence depend on truths not determined by God, while its Catholic soteriology differs independently from Reformed justification and perseverance. docs.text: Pentecostal Pioneers Pentecostalism has multiple origins in Holiness, healing, revival, Black church, missionary, and global indigenous networks. Charles Fox Parham and William J. Seymour are important pioneers, not a complete founder story. Charles Fox Parham Dates: 1873–1929 Role: Holiness evangelist and early Pentecostal pioneer At Bethel Bible School in Topeka, Parham's circle connected tongues with Spirit baptism and helped formulate “initial evidence.” His apostolic-faith networks influenced early Pentecostal teaching. His racism and later contested reputation require explicit acknowledgment; historical importance is not moral endorsement. William J. Seymour Dates: 1870–1922 Role: African American Holiness preacher and leader of the Azusa Street revival Seymour carried a Holiness-Pentecostal message to Los Angeles in 1906. The Apostolic Faith Mission's interracial worship, testimony, missionary traffic, and periodical made Azusa Street a global catalyst. Seymour emphasized repentance, justification, sanctification, Spirit baptism, divine healing, and expectant response to grace. Parham influenced Seymour, but Seymour transformed the message in a community with distinct racial, ecclesial, and missionary significance. Naming Parham alone as founder erases this development and the many independent global receptions. docs.text: John Wesley John Wesley turns the priority of grace and the reality of response into a practical theology of awakening, justification, assurance, sanctification, and perseverance. Historical context Dates: 1703–1791 Tradition: Anglican priest; principal organizer and formative theologian of Methodism Context: evangelical revival, societies and classes, debates with Calvinist Methodists, Anglican sacramental life Major works The Standard Sermons ; Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament ; journals; “Predestination Calmly Considered”; “A Plain Account of Christian Perfection.” Anthropology and prevenient grace Wesley affirms that fallen people are dead in sin and cannot make the least saving movement until God works. He then argues that every person receives some measure of preventing or prevenient grace. This grace awakens conscience and enables response without making the response inevitable. inability → prevenient grace → enabled response → faith/new birth ↘ resistance remains possible The sequence is conceptual. Wesley does not reduce grace to a detachable power possessed independently of the Spirit. Justification, new birth, and sanctification Justification is pardon and acceptance by grace through faith; new birth is interior renewal. Sanctification continues grace's transformation of desire and action. Christian perfection is perfect love excluding voluntary sin as a reigning principle, not omniscience, freedom from mistake, or independence from grace. Election and universal grace Wesley rejects unconditional reprobation and argues that the grace of God is free for all. Election is conditional and Christ-centered. His polemic is pastoral as well as metaphysical: he fears that unconditional predestination obscures God's universal love and discourages holy response. Perseverance and apostasy Wesley teaches that a true believer can make shipwreck of faith. Present assurance is real witness of the Spirit; perseverance remains dependent on continuing, grace-enabled faith and use of the means of grace. Position across the dimensions Dimension Wesley Alternatives Restored for saving response by grace Fallen ability Total inability apart from grace Grace priority Universal prevenient grace Grace resistible Yes Conversion Synergistic after enabling grace Election Conditional, in Christ Apostasy Possible Modern comparison Libertarian-leaning Influence Charles Wesley's hymns, John William Fletcher's polemical theology, and Methodist conferences help consolidate the tradition. Wesleyan teaching shapes the Holiness movement and many Pentecostal streams, though neither later movement simply repeats Wesley. Common misunderstandings Prevenient grace is not natural moral neutrality. Wesley does not teach salvation by works; even good desire flows from grace. Perfect love does not remove creaturely weakness or the need for atonement. Arminian Methodism is not identical to all Remonstrant theology. docs.text: Anabaptist / Mennonite Summary Anabaptism was a diverse sixteenth-century family rather than one theology. Mennonite trajectories emphasize God's saving grace, voluntary faith, new birth, believer's baptism, discipleship, communal discernment, and obedience. These emphases are often synergistic, but must not be equated with Pelagianism. Human nature and grace Anabaptist writers oppose inherited church membership and insist on living response to the gospel. This is not necessarily a denial of sin or grace. Contemporary Mennonite confession calls salvation God's gift through Christ and describes human response as yielding to grace, trusting God, repenting, joining the redeemed community, and living the obedience of faith. Conversion and discipleship Faith is inseparable from following Jesus, enemy-love, truthfulness, economic sharing, and baptismal allegiance. Regeneration is therefore not merely an invisible causal event; it becomes visible in a Spirit-empowered community. Election and perseverance Election and decretal predestination are usually not organizing centers. Many Mennonite accounts allow apostasy and stress enduring discipleship. Historical Anabaptists differ too much for a single formula. Free-will dimensions Dimension Common Mennonite emphasis Fallen saving ability Salvation depends on divine grace Grace priority Yes Human response Real, voluntary, communal Conversion Commonly synergistic Election Usually not framed as unconditional individual decree Apostasy Commonly possible Modern comparison Often libertarian-leaning; not confessionally analytic Formative figures and diversity Menno Simons is a major consolidator, not founder of all Anabaptism. Conrad Grebel, Felix Manz, and Balthasar Hubmaier represent different Swiss and South German trajectories; they are not interchangeable. Hubmaier wrote explicitly on freedom of the will, whereas other figures center ecclesiology and discipleship. Common misunderstandings Anabaptism is not reducible to a generic “free-will Protestantism.” Obedient discipleship is not presented as earning God's initial grace. Modern Mennonite confessions should not be retrojected unchanged onto every sixteenth-century group. docs.text: Anglican Summary Anglicanism has no single founder or single free-will theory. Its classical formularies deny unaided saving ability and affirm preventing and cooperating grace, but Reformed, Arminian, High Church, Wesleyan, and Anglo-Catholic streams develop those commitments differently. Human nature and the Fall Article IX treats original sin as corruption affecting every person. Article X says fallen people cannot turn and prepare themselves for faith by natural strength and good works. This distinguishes ordinary responsibility from saving ability. Grace and conversion Article X speaks of grace “preventing us, that we may have a good will,” and “working with us, when we have that good will.” Reformed Anglicans read conversion monergistically; Arminian and later Anglo-Catholic streams emphasize enabled cooperation. The Book of Common Prayer locates grace within proclamation, baptism, Eucharist, and prayer. Election and predestination Article XVII affirms predestination to life in Christ and treats it as comfort while warning against destructive speculation. It does not settle every later dispute over conditionality, reprobation, or perseverance, enabling competing historical receptions. Perseverance and apostasy Anglican answers differ. Reformed streams affirm preservation; Arminian, Wesleyan, and Catholic-leaning streams permit final apostasy. No single row should be attributed to the entire Communion. docs.text: Baptist Summary Baptist history contains multiple soteriological streams. General Baptists developed in an Arminian direction; Particular Baptists adopted Reformed confessions. docs.text: Roman Catholic Summary Roman Catholic teaching affirms created freedom, the damage of original sin, the absolute priority of grace, genuine cooperation in justification and sanctification, predestination, and the possibility of falling from grace. It permits several schools on how divine causality and free action fit together. Human nature and the Fall Human freedom is rooted in reason and will and grounds responsibility. Original sin deprives humanity of original holiness and wounds rather than destroys nature; freedom is weakened and inclined toward evil. The Catechism §§1730–1742 describes freedom as perfected in the good, not as mere indifference. Grace Grace is free, undeserved divine help and participation in divine life. It precedes preparation and response. The Catechism teaches both that the Spirit's initiative elicits response and that a person can reject inspiration. Grace heals and elevates rather than competing with creaturely causation. Conversion The Council of Trent and the Catechism describe adults as moved and aided by prevenient grace, freely assenting, and receiving justification as forgiveness and interior renewal. Cooperation is not an independent contribution that earns the initial gift. Baptism is the ordinary sacramental context of justification and new birth. Election and predestination Catholic teaching affirms predestination within providence and denies that God predestines anyone to hell. It does not dogmatically impose one explanation of the relation among predestination, grace, foreknowledge, and free acts. Perseverance and apostasy Sanctifying grace can be lost through mortal sin; repentance and sacramental reconciliation restore communion. Final perseverance is itself a grace to be hoped and prayed for, not a naturally guaranteed possession. Free-will dimensions Dimension Typical Catholic teaching Alternatives/sourcehood Real created agency; metaphysical analysis varies Fallen spiritual ability Cannot attain saving life without grace Grace required/prior Yes Grace resistible Yes; sufficient/efficacious relation disputed by school Divine determination Strong providence with real secondary causation Election Predestination affirmed; no predestination to evil Apostasy Possible Modern comparison No single Catholic position Internal schools Thomist/Bañezian accounts emphasize intrinsically efficacious divine motion and physical premotion while defending voluntary secondary causation. Molinism uses middle knowledge and counterfactuals of creaturely freedom to coordinate providence with libertarian choice. Augustinian and Congruist variants add further options. The Church did not resolve the de auxiliis controversy by condemning either Thomist or Molinist orthodoxy. See Aquinas and Molina . Common misunderstandings Catholicism does not teach unaided self-salvation. Synergy is not a 50/50 division of merit. “Catholicism is libertarian” ignores its permitted metaphysical schools. Predestination is affirmed, while predestination to evil or damnation is rejected. Reformed Assessment Catholic theology's strongest contribution is its sophisticated integration of grace, created secondary causation, sacrament, and moral formation; Thomist/Bañezian and Molinist theories must not be conflated. From a confessional Reformed perspective, its principal weaknesses lie in a different doctrine of justification and grace-enabled merit, the grounding burden carried by Molinist middle knowledge, and a perseverance account in which sanctifying grace can be forfeited. See Why Catholic Accounts Are Weaker from a Reformed Perspective . docs.text: Eastern Orthodox Summary Eastern Orthodox theology commonly presents freedom within creation in God's image, ancestral sin, sacramental healing, synergy, and theosis. It strongly affirms divine initiative and genuine response but does not define itself through modern libertarian/compatibilist categories. Human nature and the Fall “Ancestral sin” commonly emphasizes mortality, corruption, disordered passions, and solidarity with Adam. Orthodox writers vary in how they discuss inherited culpability and Western “original sin.” Human nature remains God's good creation but needs liberation and healing in Christ. Grace Grace is the uncreated divine life and action by which human beings are healed and brought into communion with God. It is not merely external information or a neutral opportunity. Prayer, sacrament, ascetic struggle, and virtue are modes of a grace-sustained life. Conversion Synergy names cooperation between divine grace and human response. God initiates, sustains, and brings to completion; the human person's consent and participation are real. The model is better imagined as healed participation than as two causes supplying percentages. Election and predestination Orthodox theology affirms foreknowledge and providence while commonly rejecting unconditional reprobation or a decree that makes sin necessary. John of Damascus distinguishes divine foreknowledge from predetermination of matters “in our power.” Modern Orthodox authors do not all formulate election in the same way. Perseverance and apostasy A believer must persevere in repentant communion; apostasy is possible. Confidence rests in God's faithfulness and mercy rather than a doctrine that every regenerate person must infallibly persevere. Free-will dimensions Dimension Representative Orthodox emphasis Alternatives/sourcehood Genuine created response; often libertarian-leaning Fallen spiritual ability Nature corrupted and unable to heal itself Grace required/prior Yes Grace resistible Yes Conversion Synergistic, sacramental, participatory Election Providence and foreknowledge without deterministic emphasis Apostasy Possible Modern comparison Not officially defined in analytic terms Formative theologians The tradition has no single founder. Key patristic sources include Athanasius, the Cappadocians, John Chrysostom, Maximus the Confessor , and John of Damascus . Gregory Palamas is important for later accounts of participation in divine energies. Maximus's distinction between natural and gnomic willing is Christological and ascetic, not a restatement of libertarianism. See the glossary . Internal diversity and caution Jurisdictions share liturgy, councils, and patristic inheritance, not a single modern systematic manual on free will. Representative modern writers may illuminate the tradition but should not be treated as speaking alone for all Orthodoxy. This page therefore avoids claims about a uniquely “official Orthodox theory” of causal determination. Reformed Assessment Orthodoxy's strongest contribution is its relational and participatory account of grace, healed freedom, sacrament, and theosis. From a confessional Reformed perspective, synergy leaves the final differentiating response less fully explained, its anthropology gives less weight to Augustinian-Reformed moral inability, and unconditional election and effectual calling carry less causal force. This assessment does not identify Orthodoxy with Pelagianism. See Why the Orthodox Synergistic Account Is Weaker . docs.text: Lutheran Summary Confessional Lutheranism distinguishes ordinary civil agency from the fallen person's inability to cause conversion. The Holy Spirit alone creates faith through Word and sacrament; grace is universal and can be resisted, and believers can fall away. This combination differs from both Reformed and Arminian systems. Human nature and the Fall The Augsburg Confession and Formula of Concord teach deep original corruption and inability in “spiritual things.” They do not deny reason, voluntary outward action, or civil righteousness. Formula II explicitly says the controversy is not about choices in temporal life. Grace The Spirit works through the external Word, baptism, absolution, and the Supper. The gospel is genuinely offered; conversion is not produced by an unaided capacity or a small human contribution. God's action changes an unwilling person into a willing believer. Conversion Conversion is monergistic: Scripture attributes its beginning and completion entirely to the Spirit. After conversion, the renewed will cooperates in sanctification, always dependently. Lutheran monergism therefore concerns a defined act, not the denial of all subsequent human action. Election and predestination Formula XI teaches eternal election to salvation in Christ as a source of comfort. It directs readers to Word and sacraments rather than a hidden symmetrical decree and denies that God causes sin or wills damnation. Condemnation is traced to sin, unbelief, and resistance. Perseverance and apostasy Grace can be resisted and faith can be lost. Lutheran teaching therefore combines monergistic conversion with the possibility of apostasy—evidence that “monergism” does not automatically entail Reformed perseverance. Free-will dimensions Dimension Confessional Lutheran emphasis Ordinary agency Real in temporal/civil matters Fallen saving ability None by natural powers Grace required/prior Yes; Spirit through means of grace Conversion Monergistic Grace resistible Yes Election To salvation in Christ, not symmetrical reprobation Apostasy Possible Modern comparison Difficult to map simply Formative theologians and diversity Martin Luther frames the Erasmus dispute; Philip Melanchthon shapes the Augsburg Confession and changes some later formulations; Martin Chemnitz is central to confessional consolidation. Confessional Lutheran churches also differ from liberal and other Lutheran bodies in the contemporary authority assigned to the Book of Concord. Common misunderstandings Luther did not claim that humans lack wills or make no ordinary choices. Lutherans are not “Calvinists with sacraments”: universal grace, means of grace, election, resistance, and apostasy differ. Monergistic conversion does not make preaching and sacrament dispensable; they are the Spirit's instruments. Reformed Assessment Confessional Lutheranism is one of the closest alternatives because it strongly preserves bondage of the fallen will, monergistic conversion, and the external means of grace. From a confessional Reformed perspective, the conjunction of monergistic conversion, resistible universal grace, possible apostasy, and an intentionally non-symmetrical account of election leaves a tension that effectual calling and perseverance resolve more systematically. See Why Lutheranism Comes Close but Remains Weaker . Confessional sources Augsburg Confession XVIII Apology XVIII Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration II Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration XI

docs.text: Pentecostal Summary Pentecostalism arose through several holiness, revival, and Finished Work networks; it has no single founder and no uniform free-will theory. Many classical Pentecostal bodies inherit Wesleyan or Arminian themes: human inability, universal grace, responsible faith, resistibility, and possible apostasy. Human nature, grace, and conversion The Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths teaches a voluntary Fall producing spiritual death and locates humanity's only hope in Christ. Salvation is received through repentance and faith, with regeneration and renewal attributed to the Holy Spirit and justification to grace. This official statement does not define agent causation or announce a modern libertarian theory. “Libertarian-leaning” describes a common affinity, not a confessional metaphysic. Election and perseverance Classical Pentecostal theology commonly uses conditional-election and conditional-security frameworks. The Assemblies of God explicitly rejects unconditional security and warns that a believer can fall away, while grounding assurance in a living relation with Christ. Free-will dimensions Dimension Common classical Pentecostal emphasis Saving ability unaided No Grace priority Yes Grace resistible Yes Conversion Usually Arminian/Wesleyan synergy Election Usually conditional Apostasy Possible Modern comparison Often libertarian-leaning, not officially analytic Pioneers and diversity Charles Fox Parham promoted an early doctrine of tongues as initial evidence and led the Topeka revival; his historical role must be discussed alongside his racism and contested legacy. William J. Seymour's Azusa Street mission became a far more influential interracial and global center. Holiness-Pentecostal, Finished Work, Oneness, Reformed-charismatic, and global indigenous movements differ substantially. See Pentecostal Pioneers . docs.text: Reformed / Presbyterian Summary Confessional Reformed theology teaches voluntary creaturely action under comprehensive providence, total inability in saving matters, unconditional election, effectual calling, justification by faith, and God's preservation of the saints. Later Reformed accounts are commonly compatibilist, though the confessions do not endorse one modern analytic theory. Human nature and the Fall The will retains “natural liberty” and is not forced by an absolute necessity of nature. After the Fall, however, a person cannot convert or prepare themselves for spiritual good accompanying salvation. This is inability of disposition and spiritual condition, not absence of deliberation. Grace and conversion The outward gospel call addresses many and can be rejected. In effectual calling God enlightens the mind, renews the will, and draws the elect so that they come willingly. Regeneration is commonly treated as logically prior to faith; faith is the response produced by renewing grace. Election and predestination Election is unconditional and not grounded in foreseen faith. Reprobation is usually formulated asymmetrically: Westminster speaks of passing by and ordaining to judgment for sin, while Reformed theologians differ on supra-/infralapsarian ordering and the mode of divine causality. This is not a symmetrical claim that God produces faith and unbelief in the same moral way. Perseverance Those truly united to Christ are preserved and persevere. They can fall into serious sin and lose assurance for a time, but not totally and finally lose saving grace. The Canons of Dort ground perseverance in divine mercy and use of means. Free-will dimensions Dimension Confessional Reformed emphasis Alternatives Not normally required for responsibility Sourcehood/voluntariness Strong; providence does not make creatures coerced Fallen saving ability None by natural strength Grace Effectual for the elect Conversion Monergistic Election Unconditional Apostasy Not final for the truly regenerate Modern comparison Commonly compatibilist Formative theologians and diversity Calvin , Theodore Beza, Francis Turretin, and Jonathan Edwards are important but not interchangeable. Reformed Baptist, Presbyterian, Continental Reformed, and Anglican Reformed traditions share family resemblances while differing on covenants, church, and sacraments. Common misunderstandings Reformed theology does not normally say people are robots; it insists that choices are voluntary and morally significant. “Irresistible grace” names successful renewal of the will, not belief by external compulsion. Predestination is not fatalism: preaching, deliberation, warning, and faith are ordained means. Reformed Self-Assessment This self-assessment states the confessional case rather than presenting it as neutral description. Principal strengths comprehensive providence with real secondary causes; decisive grace and monergistic regeneration; unconditional election and effectual calling; preservation and perseverance; compatibilist voluntary responsibility. Principal objections requiring defense the author-of-sin problem and the wider problem of evil; moral responsibility under determination; universal-saving-will passages; ultimate-sourcehood, manipulation, and transformed-desire objections. The dedicated Reformed evaluation presents the cumulative case, opposing readings, comparative costs, and these objections in full. docs.text: Wesleyan / Methodist Summary Wesleyan theology combines total inability apart from grace with universally offered prevenient grace, resistible response, justification by faith, sanctification, and the possibility of apostasy. Enabled choice is a gift, not autonomous natural power. Human nature and the Fall John Wesley describes humanity as dead in sin and unable to make the first movement toward God. This is not softened by appeal to a surviving neutral faculty. The reason hearers can respond is that none is left in a state of “mere nature”: preceding grace is already at work. Grace and conversion Total inability apart from grace ↓ Prevenient grace ↓ Restored/enabled response ↙ ↘ resist trust ↓ faith and new birth The diagram is logical, not a claim about conscious stages. Prevenient grace awakens and enables but does not ensure assent. Conversion is synergistic only after and within divine enabling. Election and predestination Wesley rejects unconditional election and reprobation. Election is normally understood as conditional on faith and centered in Christ, with God's universal saving will and foreknowledge affirmed. Perseverance and apostasy Believers can finally fall away, though God supplies all grace necessary to persevere. Assurance is a Spirit-given present confidence, not an unconditional guarantee detached from continuing faith. Sanctification Wesleyan theology gives unusual prominence to entire sanctification or Christian perfection: perfected love, not sinless omniscience or inability to err. Grace continues to heal desire and empower obedient love after justification. Free-will dimensions Dimension Wesleyan emphasis Natural saving ability None Grace priority Universal prevenient grace Alternatives Saving response enabled by grace Grace resistible Yes Conversion Synergistic within enabling grace Election Usually conditional/Christ-centered Apostasy Possible Modern comparison Libertarian-leaning Common misunderstandings Prevenient grace is not Pelagian natural ability. “Free for all” grace does not mean salvation is merited by decision. Christian perfection concerns mature love, not absolute faultlessness. Reformed Assessment Wesleyan theology's strongest contributions are its insistence on prior grace, universal gospel invitation, meaningful response, assurance, and holy love. From a confessional Reformed perspective, universal prevenient grace bears a substantial exegetical burden, the decisive-difference problem remains after equal enablement, and possible apostasy gives assurance a different ground from divine preservation. See Why the Wesleyan Solution Is Weaker . Primary and authoritative sources Wesley, “On Working Out Our Own Salvation” Wesley, “Free Grace” Wesley, “The Scripture Way of Salvation” See John Wesley
